articles.title: South Africa's Ramaphosa wins court battle over impeachment threat
articles.summary: The break-in happened in 2020, when thieves allegedly stole bundles of US dollar bills hidden inside a sofa at the farm.

blocks.text: South African President Cyril Ramaphosa has won a legal battle to overturn a report that found he may have a case to answer over the theft of large sums of cash from his private farm.

In 2022, an independent panel said Ramaphosa may have committed serious misconduct relating to the theft of $580,000 (£443,000), hidden in a sofa, at his Phala Phala game farm in the Limpopo province. He denied any wrongdoing.
Ramaphosa challenged the findings of the report in court after the Constitutional Court ruled that parliament had violated the constitution by blocking moves to impeach him.
The Western Cape high court ruled that the panel's report was unlawful and set it aside "in its entirety".

In its judgment, the court said the panel, appointed by parliament to investigate the allegations against Ramaphosa, had "misconstrued its function, the nature of the inquiry it was to conduct and the recommendation it was required to make".

"It went beyond its lawful remit ... and made several material errors of law. [Therefore] the report of the independent panel ... is declared unlawful and is reviewed and set aside in its entirety," Judge Nolwazi Mabindla-Boqwana said.
The court also declared unlawful the steps taken by parliament in relation to the report.
The ruling effectively removes the basis for the parliamentary impeachment process against Ramaphosa, although opposition parties have indicated they intend to challenge the decision.
The scandal, dubbed "Farmgate" by local media, has has dogged Ramaphosa since it emerged in 2022, when former spy chief Arthur Fraser reported the matter to police in a dossier.
Fraser, an ally of former President Jacob Zuma, accused Ramaphosa of concealing the theft from the police and tax authorities.
The break-in took place in 2020, when thieves allegedly stole bundles of US dollar bills hidden inside a sofa at the farm.
Earlier this month, two people were found guilty of the theft.
Ramaphosa confirmed that a robbery had taken place but said the money had been from the legitimate sale of buffalo from his livestock business.
Several investigations cleared him of any wrongdoing, but parliament began an impeachment proceedings in 2022 and appointed an independent panel to investigate the allegations.
The panel made a series of damaging findings, including that there was "substantial doubt about the legitimacy of the source of the currency that was stolen".
It also concluded that Ramaphosa "has a case to answer".
Ramaphosa initially challenged the report in court but withdrew his application after parliament voted against adopting its findings.
He revived the legal challenge again in May this year after the Constitutional Court, the country's highest court, ruled that parliament had acted unconstitutionally by blocking moves to impeach him.
It ordered parliament to refer the report to an impeachment committee.
In his latest challenge, Ramaphosa argued that the panel had "misconceived its mandate, misjudged the information placed before it and misinterpreted the four charges advanced against me".
The Western Cape High Court's ruling could bring the current impeachment process to an end, unless parliament successfully challenges the decision.
If they do, and the appeal is successful, the parliamentary committee would be able to examine the charges against the president and make a recommendation.
If the committee recommends impeachment, parliament would have to vote on whether to remove him from office. This would require the support of at least two-thirds majority in parliament.
Ramaphosa's Africa National Congress (ANC) has enough parliamentary seats to block such a move.
He is the first president to face impeachment proceedings under the rules introduced in 2018.

articles.title: Large bushfire threatens homes and properties on remote island off Tasmania
articles.summary:
Blaze spreads significantly across the north of Flinders Island after being started by lightning strikes

  • Get our

blocks.text: Homes and properties on a picturesque remote island are under threat from an out-of-control bushfire that has sent smoke hundreds of kilometres south.
The blaze on Flinders Island in Bass Strait spread significantly on Wednesday after being started by lightning strikes.
Some structures had been destroyed but it was too early to tell whether they were homes, the Tasmania Fire Service incident controller Steven Richardson said.
A Bureau of Meteorology post on X featured a video showing a vast column of smoke being blown south across north-east Tasmania, as northerly winds pushed the plume across Bass Strait.

blocks.caption: Authorities said it was too early to tell whether any homes had been lost in the blaze.  Photograph: Tasmania Fire Service

blocks.text: As of Wednesday night, three emergency warnings were in place, including for the coastal settlement of Killiecrankie and nearby areas Leeka, Mount Tanner, Mount Boyes and Carnacs Flat.
Some residents were warned it was too late to leave.
Roughly 3,000 hectares had been burned by the fire on Tuesday, before it spread south on Wednesday following a wind change.
Residents on the island, which is about 130,000 hectares in size and home to 900 people, posted photos of massive plumes of smoke on social media.
Mick Grimshaw, a farmer, helped friends move cattle from their property and said they had lost some fences.
“We were under the ashes. Right there. But we’ve got them safe,” he told ABC radio.
“The fire threat for this farm looks like it has abated a bit but certainly not further down the island.
“We can see the smoke front heading right down the guts of the island.”
after newsletter promotion

blocks.caption: A ringtail possum near the burnt-out bush on Flinders Island. Photograph: Tasmania Fire Service

blocks.text: Nearly 40 firefighters were working to control the bushfire, plus 12 parks and wildlife staff, five helicopters and three aircraft.
“Additional resources are being deployed and Tasmania Police is also helping evacuate people, particularly in the Leeka and Mount Tanner areas,” parks minister Nick Duigan said.
“There is a lot of smoke in the area and it’s now coming down Tasmania’s coast.”
Several roads have been closed because of poor visibility due to smoke.
Flinders Island is known for high-quality exports, including beef, lamb, wool and seafood.

articles.title: Suspected North Korean computer programmers did contract work for B.C. government
articles.byline: Matthew Pierce, Scott Anderson, Mark Kelley

image.caption: A man going by the name Kevin Zhang, who worked for the B.C. government, had these two fake Chinese passports in an online account. (kzdev420 / GitHub)

blocks.text: Four computer programmers who did contract work for the British Columbia government were likely North Korean operatives, CBC's the fifth estate has learned.
Between 2023 and 2025, the four were hired to work on the province’s business registry platform.

As part of a contract worth hundreds of thousands of dollars to supply the province with software developers, an IT staffing firm based in B.C.’s Lower Mainland facilitated the hiring of a man calling himself Kevin Zhang.

"Kevin's resume was ideal for the situation that I was dealing with," said the owner of the staffing firm. He spoke with the fifth estate on the condition that he and his company not be named. He said due to the nature of remote hiring, he was completely unaware he hired likely North Koreans.
Over the last year, the fifth estate has been investigating North Korean IT workers and how they, like Zhang, have been able to infiltrate Canadian businesses and government.
"With Zhang, he's pretty known," said Michael Barnhart, a former U.S. Army intelligence officer who investigates North Korea for the private sector.

"I had tracked him before. There's a couple crypto companies that had tracked him before. A couple of other just different industries that had been tracking him. And everyone had a different piece of the puzzle."
The photo from Kevin Zhang’s website, left, does not match that of the passports saved to his GitHub account, right. (kzdev420/GitHub)
Alongside the confirmation of experts like Barnhart, the fifth estate found multiple online clues that point toward North Korean IT worker tradecraft:

In an online profile Zhang used to do work for the B.C. government, he stored two fake Chinese passports. The place of birth for the holder is the Chinese province of Liaoning, which directly borders North Korea. The U.S. Department of the Treasury has previously sanctioned companies operating IT worker cells in Liaoning.

items: Watch the full documentary, "For Hire: North Korea's IT Army" from the fifth estate on YouTube, CBC Gem or CBC-TV on Friday at 9 p.m.

blocks.text: The names on the passports appear to have been modified, with neither matching the name on the bottom stripe of the document.
A resumé-style website for Zhang contained a headshot that did not match the photo on the passports.
"This is the same guy that also goes by Kevin Chang, too," Barnhart said. "Sometimes he’ll only go by that.
"Chang, Ching or Zhang, just different variations of the beginning or ending name."

As time went on, the B.C. government hired three more remote developers via the same IT staffing firm. The owner of the firm told the fifth estate that each was recommended by Zhang, who said they were former colleagues.
The owner said the B.C. government made the ultimate decision to hire them and would have conducted a 30-minute interview focused on competency.

The fifth estate reached out to multiple people and entities within the B.C. government, but received no response or was told that because of the provincial election, which concluded Oct. 24, the government would not be able to provide a response.

In response to a freedom of information request, the fifth estate was told that the ministry where Zhang worked could not locate an employee by that name, despite having been provided the account details that logged his specific contributions to a ministry software project.
Red flags
Beyond the fake Chinese passports and differing headshots, an investigation of Zhang and his colleagues conducted by the fifth estate revealed numerous other oddities.
For instance, a resumé for Zhang found online, which listed the B.C. government as a prior employer, stated his address was "Main St. E, North Bay, ON," with the street number absent.
In email correspondence provided to the fifth estate by the B.C. staffing firm, Zhang and the other developers can be seen repeatedly changing their banking information.

"In retrospect, there's a highly unusual situation to have somebody change their bank, change their company," the B.C. staffing firm’s owner said. "I think in the years that I've been doing this, right, this happened once before, twice before."
This is a red flag, according to cybersecurity expert Barnhart.

"I’ve had the same bank account at my employer for decades. I’ve never told my company to change it, ever. If I have, it would have been once. If I’d have done it twice, that would have been like: 'What are you doing?’"

At one point last year, Zhang asked to be paid to the bank account for a company called Dev Dragon Inc. Corporate records show Dev Dragon, now defunct, was registered by a James Zhang at a derelict building in Dawson City, Yukon.
The registered address for DevDragon Inc. was a long-abandoned bank building in Dawson City, Yukon. (CBC)

One of the other remote workers, Brandon Galli, had a similarly confusing digital footprint. On the account connected to his position working on B.C. government code, Galli’s profile photo is of an Asian man. However, his closely linked personal website provides a photo of a Caucasian man.
In an email obtained by the fifth estate, Galli asked for his pay to go to the account of an Ontario company called Luk Castle Investments, registered to a home in Markham by a man named Kenny Luk.
According to his LinkedIn, Luk did computer programming jobs for a number of Canadian banks before starting a software development consultancy.

When the fifth estate contacted Luk to ask about Brendan Galli and the money paid to him, he said that "Luk Castle Investments does not participate in media inquiries or respond to unsolicited questions regarding its business activities. Neither I nor anyone associated with the company will be providing comment on this matter."
It is a common practice for North Korean IT workers to use a real person’s identity to commit their fraud. (GitHub/Brandongalli.io)
The fifth estate tracked down the real Brandon Galli in New Jersey. When told that someone using his identity had worked for the B.C. government, he said his identity might have been stolen.
But pressed further, he admitted he gave his identity to someone he was working with online. He said this person continues to use his identity without his permission, causing him a host of problems.

items: Ontario architect's seal forged by remote worker believed to be North Korean fraudster
Binance says $6.3B US hacked in what could be largest cryptocurrency theft ever

blocks.text: "It was before the pandemic. We were working together on upwork and freelancing platforms and I was receiving small payouts for a short time while I was in college just to pay for food," Galli told the fifth estate in a WhatsApp message.
Barnhart has seen this same pattern play out before.
"You'll see them targeting college students a lot that might need some money," he said.

"Where it's like: 'Hey, I don't want anything from you, I just need — can I use your LinkedIn profile? Can I use your driver's licence to try to get this job one time?’ And then once you [let them use it] one time, they have it forever."

articles.title: Can AI chatbots really help shoppers find the best deals?
articles.summary: Canadians are increasingly turning to AI chatbots to help them shop, compare items, scope out discounts and, in some cases, even make purchases. But are shoppers really seeing the best deals?

image.caption: As part of a daily alert set up by ChatGPT, Monique Welter found the smartwatch she was looking to buy for her husband — selling at a 30 per cent discount. (Hugo Levesque/CBC)

blocks.text: With Black Friday deals popping up everywhere, Monique Welter used ChatGPT to set up a daily alert to find a Garmin Instinct 3 smartwatch for less than $400.
"I was pretty shocked with the last deal it sent me because, even before Black Friday, it was 30 per cent off," she said. "Usually, famous brands don't need to go that deep in discounts."
The chatbot referred her to Sail, a Canadian outdoor equipment retailer she hadn’t even considered, which was selling the watch for $350.
Monique Welter regularly uses AI chatbots Claude and ChatGPT for wardrobe recommendations and to find Black Friday deals. (Hugo Levesque/CBC)

As the holiday shopping season ramps up, more Canadians are turning to AI chatbots such as ChatGPT, Claude, Gemini and Muse to help them pick a gift at a good price point. A Deloitte survey of more than 1,000 Canadians found that 39 per cent of respondents were planning to use AI to help them shop ahead of the holidays this year, including to find deals — up from 25 per cent the year before.

"We're really seeing a lot of price comparison work being done through AI chatbots, comparing between retailers, tracking the best price of a specific item across a range of retailers, and also looking for promo codes," Calgary-based retail consultant Jeff Doucette said.
But whether those bots are turning up the best prices is another question.

"It's not actually looking [through] the whole internet. It's looking for stuff that is available to AI," Montreal shopper Étienne Parent points out. "Amazon, for example, prevents bots from looking through it."
As shoppers change the way they search, buyers and businesses worry smaller shops — and potentially better deals — might be missing from their recommendations.
But AI firms and retail experts say there are ways for businesses to make sure they show up, and for consumers to find the product they're looking for.
How products get picked up by AI
Doucette says some of the best deals out there might never be picked up by chatbots.

Search engine optimization has long been a strategy for retailers, but now they're optimizing for AI search. If the shops with the best deals haven't done the work to make their websites visible to bots, retailers and consumers might both lose out.

"If you're not cited in the AI search engines, then you're not alive in the selection of choices from a consumer perspective," said Doucette, the founder and general manager of shopper research company Field Agent Canada.

Amazon released its own AI-powered assistant Alexa for Shopping earlier this month — but the e-commerce giant also quietly blocked rival AI bots from accessing information on its site. CBC News reached out to Amazon for comment, but the company did not respond.
Retail expert Jeff Doucette says consumers often use AI chatbots to compare prices and Black Friday sales across retailers, while also looking for promotional codes. (Ryan McLeod/CBC)

A recent analysis from AI research company Vaer AI and commissioned by point-of-sale and e-commerce platform Lightspeed found that AI recommendations from a number of chatbots favoured large retailers over smaller, local ones about 90 per cent of the time when relying on its own training data, and roughly half the time when live web search was enabled.
OpenAI, the company behind ChatGPT, told CBC News in an email that items from small businesses can show up next to options from bigger chains.

"As an example, our partnership with Shopify also helps shoppers discover products from its merchants, including small businesses, and sends shoppers directly to those stores when they click through," spokesperson Taya Christianson said.

Google, which operates Gemini, says its AI tools pull information from websites and businesses of all sizes, tapping into more than 60 billion products, including descriptions, special promotions and inventory levels.

"So if you're a retailer who is keeping your product feed in the Merchant Centre refreshed, you certainly will have the opportunity to show up," said Jamie Gargatsougias, head of retail at Google Canada.
Anthropic (which operates Claude) and Meta (Muse) did not respond to a request for comment from CBC News.
'People shop over a billion times a day and discovery on Google is applicable to businesses of all sizes,' Google Canada's head of retail Jamie Gargatsougias told CBC News. (Claude Beaudoin/CBC)
Retailers like Aldo have started to change their websites to adapt to the new ways shoppers are looking for products with AI.

The shoemaker's chief information officer, Matthieu Houle, says search used to be simple — shoppers would type in keywords, like the colour and style of shoes they were looking for, and sift through options from there.
With AI, shoppers are having a conversation with a chatbot instead.
"Now the consumers are asking more, 'Hey … I'm going to a holiday party at the office. This is what I'm gonna wear. Can you recommend me a shoe?'" Houle said.

On Aldo's end, that means providing more description about a product, as well as context about where someone might wear a pair of shoes or what to match them with, to make sure they show up in AI results.

Those changes, plus Aldo's use of Shopify's tools, which help agents and chatbots discover products, make Houle confident that Aldo is showing up in AI search. But he's not convinced by the technology’s deal-finding power just yet.
"Is [AI] a deal-hunting machine? Not in my experience so far," Houle said.
Aldo's chief information officer Matthieu Houle says AI is not quite a 'deal-hunting machine' yet. (Charles Contant/CBC)
How to find the product you want
Several retailers have launched AI-powered shopping assistants to help consumers navigate their websites.

Walmart recently launched its "Sparky" agent in Canada. Loblaw integrated its PC Express grocery delivery service with ChatGPT. Canadian Tire offers the "CeeTee" assistant to guide customers through tire comparisons, recommendations and store inventory checks.

Earlier this month, Google, in partnership with retailers including Lululemon, Shoppers Drug Mart and Simons, rolled out a new tool that lets users buy things with an AI chatbot, practically replacing the online checkout process.

Santo Ligotti, vice-president of marketing at the Retail Council of Canada, says consumers should revise their AI prompts — and the links they provide to the chatbot — to make sure they’re finding the right product at the right price. He says AI sometimes draws upon inaccurate information, fake reviews and outdated pricing.
"I think it's important to be clear about … what it is that you're asking for and making sure that you're reviewing that information," he said.
That’s something Monique Welter did when searching for a discounted smartwatch.

"I did in the beginning get a few alerts that, when I opened the link, weren't exactly the price it was saying it was," said the Toronto resident, who also uses AI to help with wardrobe recommendations.
Ligotti suggests also asking chatbots if there has been a trend of users returning the product. To state the obvious: The cheapest item may not necessarily be of the best quality.
While AI search results may not be perfect, many shoppers say chatbots save them "a lot of time" by cutting through all the Black Friday and Cyber Monday noise.
"Instead of going to five different websites, AI will do it for me in, like, three seconds," said Marc-Antoine Laporte, an avid online shopper based in Rimouski, Que.
As the old saying goes: Time is money.

articles.title: Yes, COVID cases are on the rise again. And yes, experts say, it's still a very good idea to get vaccinated
articles.summary: Infectious disease specialists say there's plenty of reason to get the COVID-19 vaccine to reduce risk of severe infection, either for yourself or someone around you who may be at higher risk.

image.caption: The number of COVID-19 cases across Canada is relatively low but rising, according to government data. While the days of the pandemic are past, there are several good reasons to get a vaccine, experts say. (Jeff Stapleton/CBC)

blocks.text: The COVID-19 vaccine is probably not in your mind the way it was when the global pandemic was in full swing.

But given this year's influenza season is off to an early start — and that respiratory viruses could already be causing school and work absences in your household — you may be wondering if it's time to think about getting an updated shot.
Here's what you need to know.
How common is COVID right now?
The Canadian respiratory virus surveillance report on COVID-19 shows that for the week of Nov. 14, the most recent for which data is available, there were 2,170 laboratory confirmed cases.
The number is rising from previous weeks, but that level is still considered low.
However, infectious disease specialists say there's plenty of reason to get the vaccine to reduce risk of severe infection either for yourself or someone around you who may be at higher risk.

"Some people think COVID is gone and forgotten, and it absolutely isn't," said Dr. Isaac Bogoch, a professor at the University of Toronto. "It's still a very dangerous pathogen, especially for people over the age of 80."

McMaster University professor Dawn Bowdish, who researches respiratory diseases, notes that in 2024, COVID-19 was still among the top 10 causes of death in Canada, "which I think a lot of people are surprised by."
MRNA vaccines much safer than getting COVID-19: review
Where are outbreaks happening?
According to the respiratory virus surveillance report, 61 confirmed outbreaks of COVID-19 were reported by participating provinces and territories for the week of Nov. 14.
The majority were in congregate settings like acute care (52 per cent) and long-term care facilities (33 per cent).
Who should get the COVID-19 vaccine this fall?

Canada's National Advisory Committee on Immunization (NACI) strongly recommends the vaccine for anyone who is at increased risk of exposure to the SARS-CoV-2 virus or who is vulnerable to severe COVID-19 disease.
That includes everyone over the age of 65 and those living in long-term care or in other congregate settings like retirement homes.

NACI also strongly recommends vaccination for those over the age of six months who have underlying health conditions that put them at higher risk of severe infection, as well as health-care workers and others employed in community settings.
Those who are pregnant, or who are from First Nations, Inuit, Métis and other equity-denied communities are also at higher risk of severe infection and should get the vaccine.

Lynora Saxinger, an infectious disease specialist and professor at the University of Alberta in Edmonton, says people sometimes underestimate their own vulnerability to severe COVID-19 infection, thinking of only the very elderly and ill as at-risk.
"But it honestly could just be someone in the community who's on cardiac medications and is 66 years old," she said.
Long COVID patients could see delays, cutbacks with changes to B.C.’s virtual care access
Can I get the vaccine if I'm not in one of those groups?
Yes. NACI says vaccines may be offered to other individuals aged six months or older based on individual risk assessment or preference.
Even if you remove the most severe outcomes from the equation, COVID disrupts schools and health-care systems, says Bowdish, "so we have the power to reduce those."
Saxinger says people in frequent contact with higher-risk people should consider getting the vaccine.

A COVID-19 infection could fly under your radar as a minor cold, but it could have "really terrible consequences" when you visit, for example, a grandparent or someone undergoing chemotherapy, Saxinger said — an important consideration heading into the holiday season.

items: Despite early start, Canada's flu season may be 'far from peak' as holidays approach

blocks.text: Another thing to ask yourself is how long it's been since your last COVID-19 vaccine.
"If your last booster was in 2022 … it's a good idea to get a repeat vaccination this season," says Saxinger.
Some provincial health ministries, including those in Quebec and Alberta, no longer make COVID-19 vaccines universally available for free, something Bowdish describes as "a huge equity issue."
Having a hard time getting the COVID-19 shot?
What will the vaccine do for me?

While the vaccine will vastly reduce your risk of getting a severe case of COVID-19, or of infecting someone else, it won't reduce your risk of catching the virus in the first place, in the way the first COVID-19 vaccines did, says Bogoch.
When the virus was brand new and the global population had no immunity whatsoever, those first vaccines were game-changers that did "a remarkable job in reducing the risk of infection," he said.
But as the different variants emerged, "the vaccines' ability to reduce the risk of infection was curtailed."
"So, really, the vaccines are there to mitigate the risks of severe infections, such as hospitalization and death," Bogoch said.
Does it matter which vaccine I get?
Right now there are two mRNA-based vaccines available in Canada — from Moderna and Pfizer — and a protein-based vaccine from Novavax.

Supply may vary based on how much of each vaccine a provincial or territorial health ministry has chosen to order. Links to appointment information for each jurisdiction can be found on this federal government hub, or you can ask your local pharmacy about which vaccines are available near you.
But Bowdish says all three vaccines have met rigorous safety standards, so there's no reason to shop around.
"The best vaccine is the one that's in your arm," she said.
However, some people may be more comfortable sticking with a vaccine they've previously had — and if that brings them back for routine immunization, that's a good thing, says Bogoch.
On the flip side, if people have been put off by flu-like symptoms they've experienced after having an mRNA vaccine, they may prefer to try Novavax instead, says Bowdish.
Health Canada approves Moderna's new mRNA shots for flu, flu-COVID combo
What about that combo vaccine?
You may have heard about a shot that combines influenza and COVID-19 vaccines.
Health Canada approved Moderna's combination mRNA vaccine earlier this month, but the company told The Canadian Press it won't reach pharmacies in time for this respiratory virus season.
Saxinger says anything that makes it easier to get immunized against respiratory viruses is a plus.
"I myself usually get [flu and COVID vaccines] at the same time, and having one sore arm instead of two seems like a bonus."

articles.title: Highest MP turnover rate in decades making for byelection bonanza this Parliament
articles.summary: A slew of MP resignations is putting this Parliament on track to have the most byelections this soon after a general election in over half a century.

image.caption: A voter casts a ballot in Toronto during a byelection in April. Voters in six federal ridings are going to the polls on Dec. 7. (Evan Mitsui/CBC)

blocks.text: Politics·New
A slew of MP resignations is putting this Parliament on track to have the most byelections this soon after a general election in over half a century.
Last time there were this many byelections this soon after a general election was 1950
· CBC News
· Posted: Nov 25, 2026 4:00 AM EST | Last Updated: 31 minutes ago

It will be 560 days since the 2025 election when voters in six ridings go to the polls on Dec. 7. That will bring the total number of byelections held since the last general election to 13 — and that doesn't include the riding of Parry Sound-Muskoka where current MP Scott Aitchison has signalled his intention to resign in the coming weeks.

The last time there were more byelections in that short amount of time was after the 1949 election. That year, newly minted Liberal Leader Louis St. Laurent won his first election as prime minister and by October of 1950 he had called 16 byelections.

Jonathan Malloy, a political science professor at Carleton University, says there are some similarities between the current Parliament and the one elected in 1949, given St. Laurent and Prime Minister Mark Carney both returned the Liberal Party to power after taking over leadership.
But beyond that, he told CBC News that "the political conditions were rather different back then."

"This is a very unusual Parliament and, to me, it's because of the unexpected election results in April 2025," Malloy said, noting that Carney's Liberals were behind in the polls when he took over the party.

"In both cases you do have a prime minister succeeding another one and successfully winning elections. That's the obvious connection. But on the other hand, the 1949 election was not radically different from what people had been expecting, say a year or two before."

Ironically, there is a near identical situation between the Terrebonne byelection held earlier this year and the 1950 byelection in what was then the Nova Scotia riding of Annapolis-Kings: both results from the preceding general election were declared void due to issues around vote counting.
But besides that case, the reasons for the rapid turnover rate in the 21st Parliament appear to be quite different from the current crop of MPs who have recently left their seats.

Of the 16 MPs who vacated in the first few years following the 1949 vote, most were appointed to judicial or Senate positions. A handful of seats were also left vacant after five MPs died while in office between October 1949 and October 1950.

Éric Grenier — a polls analyst who noted the byelection trend for his publication, The Writ — told CBC News that the amount of MPs stepping down so far in this Parliament could be "just a bit of a coincidence" because there have been a variety of reasons for their resignations.

Conservative Damien Kurek was the first MP to exit to allow for leader Pierre Poilievre to reclaim a seat. Carney also appointed former MPs Bill Blair and Jonathan Wilkinson to diplomatic posts — and appointed Richard Martel to the Senate.
Our Sunday night panel dives into a discussion on the six byelections called today

Four MPs swapped their federal roles for provincial or municipal ones. Larry Brock left to return to his local Crown attorney's office. Former cabinet ministers Steven Guilbeault and Chrystia Freeland left after serving a number of years in the former Trudeau government and Conservative Cathay Wagantall had been on the Opposition benches since 2015.

Malloy said the surprising reversal of Liberal fortunes during the 2025 campaign could have pushed some of those MPs to reassess their career trajectories. He suggested that for Liberals, they may have expected to lose their seats (or move to the Opposition benches) under Trudeau and are "not really comfortable in this new situation" of serving in Carney's government — as was the apparent case with Guilbeault.
For Conservatives, Malloy said there are likely some dashed expectations of forming government.
"Elections have a habit of helping MPs make their career decisions one way or the other," he said.
Grenier said the Liberals attaining a majority in the House earlier this year may have also factored into recent decisions.
"[That] kind of sets everybody's minds to the next four years rather than the next 18 months," he said.

The current slate of byelections may not reach the same levels as seen in the early days of Parliament when MPs were expected to resign and rerun in their riding when they were appointed ministers — a practice that was ended in 1931.
Still, Grenier says it's been a significant amount of byelections so far this parliamentary session.
"It is just kind of remarkable how many there's been," he said.
ABOUT THE AUTHOR

Darren Major is a senior writer for CBC's parliamentary bureau in Ottawa. He previously worked as a digital reporter for CBC Ottawa and a producer for CBC's Power & Politics. He holds a master's degree in journalism and a bachelor's degree in public affairs and policy management, both from Carleton University. He also holds a master's degree in arts from Queen's University. He can be reached at darren.major@cbc.ca.

articles.title: German auto workers on back foot as costs, competition bite
articles.summary: German auto workers profited during the industry's boom years, but are now increasingly being asked to trade past gains for future job security.

image.caption: The most sensitive issue for unions may be the demand that employees work more for the same amount of pay [FILE: May 20, 2022]Image: David Hecker/AFP

blocks.text: For decades, German auto bosses and labor representatives touted their ability to work through their disagreements in a uniquely cooperative process. Those days appear to be gone.
A series of crises across the industry and abrupt moves by management to slash costs are testing the limits of the German power-sharing agreement.
As negotiations between union representatives and Germany's largest carmaker, Volkswagen, began on Tuesday, the balance of power appeared increasingly one-sided.
Volkswagen wants to freeze wages for the next two years while cutting several allowances and bonuses.
Alongside Mercedes, it's demanding longer hours under the same pay, with both companies threatening to withhold investment from German factories.

Unions have responded with warning strikes and the threat of larger walkouts. Yet workers are aware of the grim outlook, with Germany's auto industry losing more than 123,000 jobs between 2019 and 2025, according to the Ifo Institute.

"I think that the labor representatives are in a very difficult situation," said Thomas Haipeter, a labor researcher at the University of Duisburg-Essen. "On the one hand, they have to make concessions in order to safeguard jobs. And despite these massive employment reductions to safeguard the rest of the jobs and locations, what is missing for them is a kind of more offensive strategy."
Can 'legacy' bring Volkswagen back from the brink?
A hot shower a day
Labor's outsized role in German auto companies goes back decades and includes a 1945 deal at Volkswagen promising a hot shower a day.
That year marks the start of "co-determination" at the company, in which workers are represented internally by employee-led workers' councils, as well as by outside labor unions.

Berlin then anchored labor's strong say in Volkswagen in 1960, before the firm issued public shares, ensuring government officials retained extra votes in the supervisory board. Those seats, belonging to the Lower Saxony government, tend to be sympathetic to workers.
Workers' councils, meanwhile, became a fixture across the German auto industry, with representation extending across multiple production sites within the same companies.
Pay and benefits for auto workers have risen over the years. During the last German industry boom, between 2011 and 2019, pay for auto workers clearly outpaced the average German wage.

In early 2025, auto workers were earning nearly a third more per hour than the typical German worker, when bonuses and allowances are factored in, according to Germany's Federal Statistical Office (Destatis).
That same year, Volkswagen CEO Oliver Blume praised cooperation with the unions as one of the company's "great strengths” during the 80-year anniversary of the 1945 agreement.
Cracks in the relationship
Cracks were long in the making, according to case studies by Haipeter and others. Labor was increasingly forced to protect plants and jobs as companies chased cheaper workers abroad.
Workers' councils turned their attention to saving their own production lines. They focused on business strategy and even hired business consultants in an effort to sway strategy.
When combustion engines dominated, autoworkers could argue German production was the most technologically advanced, according to Haipeter. That changed with the shift to electric vehicles.

"This line of compromise is canceled now by management," he said. "They say it doesn't matter for us where we produce. We have to produce at the locations or in countries which are best-cost countries and not in countries which have higher wages."
Slow sales of electric autos and competition from Chinese manufacturers have, meanwhile, exposed the cost difference.

In 2024, Volkswagen abruptly canceled a series of labor agreements and threatened factory closures. After tough negotiations, labor agreed to significant cuts — €1.5 billion yearly in abandoned wage hikes and the elimination of 50,000 positions through attrition — in exchange for job security for current employees through 2030.

Management returned this summer with a restructuring plan that included the closures of four German plants. It delayed that decision following negotiations, but slated another 50,000 positions for attrition.
Volkswagen declined to comment for this article.
Can crisis reinvent the car again?
More hours, same pay
The most sensitive issue for unions may be the demand that employees work more for the same amount of pay, or even receive less for less work.

The union IG Metall won the concession for a 35-hour workweek in 1984 after seven weeks of strikes. It's now standard in every labor contract in the auto industry, although it's not uncommon for worksites to deviate upon employee agreement, according to Haipeter.

Mercedes has called for employees to agree to an exception across the company. The company acknowledged that the 35-hour workweek was "hard-won" and "means a great deal" to its workers. "However, the conditions under which it was agreed upon no longer exist today," it said in a statement to DW.
Volkswagen, meanwhile, is demanding greater "flexibility" as the negotiations get underway.
"They call it flexibility in both directions," Thorsten Gröger, head of negotiations for the union said last week. "In the end, Volkswagen wants its employees to perform unpaid work."
The 35-hour workweek is too sacred for unions to give in, said Ferdinand Dudenhöffer, a longtime analyst of the German car industry.

"The unions are in a difficult position," he noted. "They battled for a 35-hour workweek, and that's an incredible privilege that comes with a lot of pride. The union knows that as soon as one factory, one production hall, gives up the 35-hour workweek, then they will have a conflagration."

Düdenhöffer sees parallels in another crisis from Volkswagen's history. After a downturn in the early 1990s, the then-head of the German state of Lower Saxony, Gerhard Schröder, pushed for an agreement for workers to work less in exchange for retaining their jobs.
"We need a mediator along these lines," he said.

articles.title: VP Sara questions SC dismissal of petitions challenging Rodrigo Duterte arrest
articles.summary: Vice President Sara Duterte on Wednesday decried the Supreme Court decision dismissing the petitions challenging the arrest of her father, former President Rodrigo Duterte, insisting that its…

blocks.text: Published November 25, 2026 4:50pm

Vice President Sara Duterte on Wednesday decried the Supreme Court decision dismissing the petitions challenging the arrest of her father, former President Rodrigo Duterte, insisting that its underlying issues concern national sovereignty.
The SC earlier dismissed consolidated habeas corpus petitions filed by the Vice President’s siblings—Sebastian, Veronica, and Paolo Duterte—challenging the March 2025 arrest of their father.

The High Court ruled that the petitions have become moot and that Philippine courts cannot enforce the writ because he is now in the custody of the International Criminal Court (ICC) in The Hague, Netherlands.
The Vice President, in response, said that no Philippine court should “lightly dismiss” a petition as moot.

“No foreign court or nation should ever stand above the sovereignty of our country. The protection of the life, liberty, and fundamental rights of every Filipino citizen must remain paramount,” Sara Duterte said.

“No Philippine court should lightly dismiss a petition as moot, when the underlying issues concern national sovereignty, constitutional accountability, and the government’s duty to protect the life and liberty of every Filipino from foreign interference,” she added.
A day after Rodrigo Duterte’s arrest in March 2025, his children separately filed petitions for habeas corpus, a legal remedy used to challenge unlawful detention and seek a person’s release.
The camp of Veronica “Kitty” Duterte said they will file a motion for reconsideration, following the SC decision. —AOL, GMA News

articles.title: Dancing with the Stars Season 35 Finale: Who Won the Mirrorball?
articles.summary: Dancing with the Stars crowned its winner. An unexpected moment during the final freestyle turned an already powerful performance by the winning pair into an unforgettable one, prompting a standing…

image.caption: The five finalists of Dancing With The Stars season 35. From left: actor Tatyana Ali, comedian and podcaster Connor Wood, Olympic figure skater Amber Glenn, Paralympic gold medallist Ezra Frech and reality star and model, Maura Higgins. (Andrew Eccles/Disney)

blocks.text: Entertainment·New

Dancing with the Stars crowned its winner. An unexpected moment during the final freestyle turned an already powerful performance by the winning pair into an unforgettable one, prompting a standing ovation and bringing the room to tears.
Emotional freestyles and the final results. Here's everything that went down in the finale
Warning: Spoilers ahead
Dancing with the Stars has crowned its winner.
Paralympic gold medallist Ezra Frech and his pro partner Daniella Karagach won Season 35 of the reality TV dance competition, taking home the Len Goodman Mirrorball Trophy.

But it was an unexpected moment during the final freestyle that turned an already powerful performance by the winning pair into an unforgettable one, prompting a standing ovation and bringing the room to tears.
Midway through their performance, Frech's prosthetic leg came off. The track athlete didn't miss a beat, continuing the choreography before putting it back on, and carrying on.
Frech and Karagach were in tears as their names were announced and Season 34 winners Robert Irwin and Witney Carson handed over the trophy.
"This is the most special moment of my life," Frech told the audience as his fellow cast members hoisted him into the air and confetti rained down.
'I'm just so freaking grateful," Karagach added.
Ezra Frech and Daniella Karagach won Season 35 of Dancing with the Stars, taking home the Len Goodman Mirrorball Trophy. (Eric McCandless/Disney)

For Tuesday's finale, five pairs remained: Olympic figure skater Amber Glenn and pro dancer Pasha Pashkov, comedian and podcaster Connor Wood and pro dancer Rylie Arnold, Frech, reality star Maura Higgins and dance partner Mark Ballas and actor Tatyana Ali and dancer Jan Ravnik.
The jam-packed, three-hour finale saw each couple take to the floor for three dances and the entire cast return for dazzling interludes.
The show pairs professional ballroom dancers with celebrity partners, with viewers voting alongside the judges to decide the winner.

items: Dancing with the Stars Season 35 finale: What you can expect
How Dancing with the Stars became must-watch TV in the streaming era

blocks.text: First up was the judges' choice, where a judge assigned each finalist a specific dance style and song. Then came the instant dance, where couples found out their style and song just moments before. And the freestyle, where anything goes — think of it as their Superbowl halftime show, their pop star moment.

For their freestyle, Frech and Karagach danced to Linkin Park's Numb, paying tribute to people with disabilities, drawing on the Paralympian's own experiences. The two danced alongside an ensemble of dancers in wheelchairs.
Frech began the routine without his prosthetic leg before disappearing behind a wall to put it on and rejoin Karagach on the dance floor.

But when Frech's prosthetic came off on the dance floor, he rallied and quickly put it back on. The pair finished with Karagach balancing on his prosthetic as Frech held a bedazzled one in the air, earning a standing ovation and some of the loudest applause of the night.
"If one person with a disability feels more confident and holds their head up high because of this show then ive done my job." he said, before scoring perfect 10s.
The judges were moved.
Derek Hough called Frech "incredible," saying the performance would have a "ripple effect far beyond this show" and praising how he rose to the moment.
Bruno Tonioli declared him "a national treasure," describing the routine as a "powerful, beautiful, life-affirming statement."
And Carrie Ann Inaba, made sure Karagach got her flowers too, saying, "Dani, we need to salute you" for creating a "whole new vocabulary for dance."
Frech and Karagach scored perfect 10s throughout the night—in both the judge's salsa choice to Danza Kuduro by Don Omar and surprise tango to Levels by Avicii.
Here's how the other finalists finished, and a look back at their final performances.

Score: 90/90

Third place: Connor Wood and Rylee Arnold
Score: 82/90
Judges' choice: Viennese Waltz to Willing and Able by Noah Kahan.
Instant: Cha-cha to Buttons, The Pussycat Dolls

Freestyle: A Tom Holland-styled, Lip Sync Battle-inspired performance to Gene Kelly's Singin’ in the Rain and Rihanna's Umbrella. Yes they actually danced in the rain and yes he ripped off his shirt to reveal a corset.
Fourth place: Tatyana Ali and Jan Ravnik
Judges' choice: Salsa to Jamaican (Bam Bam) by Hugel & Solto

Freestyle: A sci-fi inspired performance to Minnie the Moocher by Cab Calloway and Over the Rainbow by Judy Garland, which Inaba praised as "beyond insane." Ravnik also blurted out, “I’m so f-ing proud” after the routine, prompting a bleep.

Hough called it "a beautiful button on a fantastic season."

articles.title: Fact check: Trump didn't make Marcos wait at ASEAN Summit red carpet
articles.summary: A TikTok video falsely claims Trump made Marcos wait at the ASEAN Summit.

blocks.text: November 25, 2026 | 4:46pm
MANILA, Philippines — A TikTok video falsely claims that US President Donald Trump made President Bongbong Marcos wait at the red carpet of the 2026 ASEAN Summit.
The November 16 post from user Papa De Channel claims that Trump kept Marcos, along with First Lady Liza Marcos, waiting for his arrival at the summit's red carpet.
Text placed on the video, “Trump makes Marcos wait on the red carpet for his arrival at ASEAN Summit,” emphasizes the claim.
However, the footage was obtained from the YouTube channel ShanghaiEye, affiliated with the state-owned Shanghai Media Group.
The video shows the arrival of different leaders and delegates for the opening ceremony of the 49th ASEAN Summit on November 15, greeted by Marcos and the first lady.
The date, "November 15, 2026," is visible in the upper-right corner of the video.
The Department of Foreign Affairs announced on November 11 that Trump was expected to arrive in the Philippines on November 17 for the ASEAN-US Special Summit.
Trump landed at the Ninoy Aquino International Airport on November 17.

articles.title: FACT CHECK: ICC chamber order on ‘Incident 57’ doesn’t mean Duterte will be released
articles.summary: While the ICC Trial Chamber III did order the removal of ‘Incident 57’ from the list of incidents in the charges against Duterte, this does not mean the entire case itself has been dismissed or that…

blocks.text: Claim: Former president Rodrigo Duterte is set to be released after the International Criminal Court (ICC) dropped one drug-related killing, “Incident 57,” from his crimes against humanity case.

Why we fact-checked this: The Facebook reel bearing the claim has already received 823,000 views, 12,500 reactions, 1,400 shares, and 1,200 comments as of writing. It was posted on November 17 and continues to gain traction up to this date.

The video shows a photo of Vice President Sara Duterte and her father, who is currently detained at the ICC facility in The Hague, Netherlands. The text on the photo reads, “Tuluyan nang ibinasura ng ICC ang Incident 57 drug war charges laban kay PRRD dahil sa sablay ng petsa.”(The ICC has definitively dismissed the ‘Incident 57’ drug war charges against [former president Rodrigo Roa Duterte] due to an error in the date.)
Additional text overlaid on the reel claimed that the ICC junked the case and that the Vice President has urged their supporters to pray for her father’s safety upon his supposed return.

The facts: While the ICC Trial Chamber III’s order to drop “Incident 57” from the list of incidents in the second count of charges against Duterte is genuine, it is not true that he is set to be released following this directive.
Duterte remains detained in ICC custody. There are no credible news reports or official announcements saying that Duterte can now return to the Philippines or that his case has been dismissed.

In an October 9 ruling, the ICC Trial Chamber III ordered prosecutors to remove Incident 57, a single alleged drug-related killing involving a “high-value target,” because it fell outside the confirmed timeframe of the second charge against Duterte.

The prosecution then complied with the order. In a document dated October 20, the prosecution said that all references to Incident 57 are now removed from the trial brief and replaced with redacted information.

Duterte is currently facing three counts of crimes against humanity, including murders in and around Davao City allegedly committed by the “Davao Death Squad” while he served as mayor between 2013 and 2016, targeted killings of alleged high-value targets during his presidency between 2016 and 2017, and murders and attempted murders during barangay-level anti-drug operations between 2016 and 2018.

List of incidents: Aside from Incident 57, which the ICC chamber ordered removed, there are many other active incidents included in the charges against Duterte. In October, the ICC trial chamber approved the addition of seven new incidents to the charges, raising the total number from 49 to 56.
Duterte was arrested in March 2025 for crimes against humanity. He is set to face trial on November 30.Previous fact checks: Rappler has fact-checked similar false claims about Duterte’s detention:

articles.title: Romualdez asks Sandiganbayan to reconsider 90-day suspension
articles.summary: Detained former House Speaker Martin Romualdez has filed a motion for reconsideration of the 90-day suspension imposed on him by the Sandiganbayan due to his plunder charge.

blocks.text: November 25, 2026 | 4:44pm
Photo released yesterday by the Bureau of Jail Management and Penology shows former House speaker Martin Romualdez being guarded at the Quezon City Jail.
MANILA, Philippines — Detained former House Speaker Martin Romualdez has filed a motion for reconsideration of the 90-day suspension imposed on him by the Sandiganbayan due to his plunder charge.

In a 16-page motion for reconsideration filed on November 19, Romualdez, through his legal team, argued that the preventive suspension is unwarranted, challenging the validity of the plunder charges and asserting that his ongoing detention makes the suspension entirely unnecessary.
According to Romualdez’s camp, the “information” against him failed to identify the main plunderer, yet the court failed to rule on the issue.

Citing Macapagal-Arroyo v. People, it stressed that when multiple individuals are charged with plunder, the law requires the main plunderer to be identified—either through allegations of a wheel conspiracy, an express conspiracy, or a properly alleged implied conspiracy.
“The Information does not allege that accused Romualdez, as distinguished from Co, amassed it. It alleges only that Romualdez and Co enriched 'themselves,'" Romualdez’s camp said.

Furthermore, Romualdez’s camp pointed out that the Information does not identify him as having personally received any money on the 15 alleged occasions. Instead, the charges claim the funds were received on his behalf by Joselyn Serenio and other employees before being funneled through dummy corporations to acquire properties and assets, including shares in Prime Media Holdings Inc. and DigiPlus Interactive Corp., and to fund donations to Harvard and Cornell Universities.
Romualdez’s lawyers also argued that the Ombudsman publicly prejudged the lawmaker by labeling him the "mastermind" and "master plunderer" of the scheme before the investigation concluded.

“The Questioned Resolution holds that this objection was waived when accused Romualdez entered his plea on 16 September 2026. With utmost respect, it was not. As pointed out in his Rejoinder dated 26 October 2026, accused Romualdez raised the Ombudsman's prejudgment at the very inception of the preliminary investigation, on 22 April 2026, and reiterated it on 27 April 2026. An objection raised at the earliest opportunity and consistently pursued thereafter cannot be deemed waived,” Romualdez’s camp said.
He also pointed out that the primary purpose of a preventive suspension is to prevent an official from using his office to influence witnesses, tamper with evidence, or commit further malfeasance.
With the former House speaker already detained in Quezon City, he argued that he is already restricted from performing any legislative functions.
"A preventive suspension which can no longer serve its purpose is not warranted," Romualdez’s motion read.
The case stemmed from a September 4 Information charging Romualdez and his co-accused, fugitive former lawmaker Zaldy Co, with plunder.

The Ombudsman alleged that the accused amassed at least P7,440,000,000.00 in kickbacks and commissions from government infrastructure and flood control projects funded under the General Appropriations Acts from 2022 to 2025.
The former House speaker, who is the president's cousin, denied all the allegations against him.

articles.title: Senate cuts P19.8B from AICS, MAP budget, reallocates to PhilHealth subsidy
articles.summary: The Senate has slashed nearly P20 billion from the allocated budget for the Assistance to Individuals in Crisis Situation (AICS) and the Medical Assistance Program (MAP) under the proposed 2027…

blocks.text: Published November 25, 2026 4:36pm

The Senate has slashed nearly P20 billion from the allocated budget for the Assistance to Individuals in Crisis Situation (AICS) and the Medical Assistance Program (MAP) under the proposed 2027 national budget.

Senate Finance panel chairman JV Ejercito announced this Wednesday, noting that the financial assistance programs each suffered a P9.9 billion reduction — which will be reallocated to Philippine Health Insurance Corporation (PhilHealth) subsidy.

With P19.8 billion reallocated, Ejercito said the budget for PhilHealth subsidy now stands at P94.2 billion, up from P73 billion initially allocated under the House-approved General Appropriations Bill (GAB).
“Ang ayuda, partly ... we will partly slash and nilagay namin ‘yung marami sa PhilHealth. Kaya Philhealth, sa subsidy will increase by almost P20 billion,” he said in an ambush interview.
(We will partially reduce the financial assistance and reallocate a significant portion to PhilHealth. The subsidy under PhilHealth will increase by nearly P20 billion.)

“P74 billion, P73 billion, magiging P94 [billion]. Ang target nga natin gawing P100 billion pero masikip ang fiscal space. So hopefully kung maabot ‘yung P100 billion para mas maganda ang subsidy ng PhilHealth,” he added.

(From P74 billion or P73 billion, it will become P94 billion. Our target was actually to reach P100 billion, but fiscal space is tight. Hopefully, we can reach that P100 billion allocation to provide a better subsidy under PhilHealth.)

The Senate Finance panel chair said that with higher subsidies for PhilHealth, there will be an increased budget for the zero balance billing, preventive care, immunization and health promotion, and for the health facilities enhancement program to improve provincial hospitals and locally funded health facilities.
“Lahat sa healthcare saka sa infrastructure, that is our priority,” Ejercito said.
(Everything related to healthcare and infrastructure, that is our priority.)
'Double funding'
Ejercito likewise committed that alleged duplicate funding for some projects will be rechecked and will be corrected if verified.
“Definitely, kapag may red flag at mga double entry, tanggal kaagad ‘yun. Syempre…humanly impossible mache-check mo, libo ‘yan. Dahan dahan, kaya nga iniisa-isa namin,” he said.

(Definitely, if there’s a red flag or a double entry, it’s removed immediately. Of course… it’s humanly impossible to check everything—there are thousands of items. We’re taking it step by step, slowly.)
“Siguro may nakakalusot. Kung may nakakalusot man, talagaang ano ‘yun, unintentional,” he added.
(It’s possible that some irregularities slipped through. If any did, it’s truly unintentional.)
Ejercito said he is seeking help from budget watchdogs and the public to help monitor any questionable items in the proposed 2027 national budget.

Senator Panfilo “Ping” Lacson earlier flagged duplicate appropriations for some flood control projects in the proposed 2027 national budget, raising fresh concerns over funding irregularities amid the ongoing controversy over anomalous flood control projects.
Lacson said the duplicate allocations were separate from at least 30 alleged ghost multipurpose buildings (MPBs) his team had identified in the proposed budget.

Lacson had also questioned the proposed appropriations for 3,950 MPBs, separate from the 1,584 MPBs covered by the Local Government Support Fund's (LGSF) Financial Assistance to local government units (LGUs) subprogram from 2022 to 2026. — RSJ, GMA News

blocks.text: Chancellor Friedrich Merz has spoken in the Bundestag as the debate opens on the government's budget plans for 2027.
"We no longer have the money for everything," Merz said in his remarks to the German parliament.

He described the tight budget, which has to be finalized this week, as an "accurate reflection" of the "difficult situation as a country — geopolitically, technologically, and demographically" that Germany finds itself in.
"We will no longer be able to afford everything with tax revenue that we have become all too accustomed to for far too long," Merz added.

The government has €560.9 billion (around $614 billion) to spend in its core budget for 2027, but both Merz's conservative CDU/CSU and the Social Democrats, who make up the coalition government, have stressed that the budget for 2028 will be even more challenging.

The extra borrowing for defense and infrastructure, that marked a break with years of debt avoidance, "is limiting our room to maneuver in the coming years to an extent that many have not yet truly come to terms with," Merz warned.

articles.title: Colombian security forces storm supermarket, free hostages
articles.summary: A failed robbery turned into a day-long hostage crisis in one of Colombia's most popular tourist destinations. The incident comes amid concerns over the deteriorating security situation in the South…

image.caption: Soldiers were deployed outside the Exito supermarket in Cartagena, where around 30 people were initially taken hostageImage: Manuel Pedraza/AFP

blocks.text: Colombian security forces stormed a supermarket in the Caribbean city of Cartagena early Wednesday, ending a day-long hostage crisis.
President Abelardo de la Espriella said all hostages had been rescued and one of the hostage-takers had been killed.
"In an extraordinary joint operation between the National Police and the Armed Forces, all the hostages were rescued," de la Espriella said.
Around 30 people had initially been taken captive at a branch of the Exito supermarket chain in Cartagena's La Castellana neighborhood.
Ten of them, including some elderly women, had already been released on Tuesday after hours of negotiations.
No further details were immediately available about whether any of the hostages had been injured.
How did the Cartagena hostage crisis unfold?
According to authorities, the hostage crisis followed a failed attempt to rob an armored vehicle transporting cash from a shopping mall.
Police, troops and special forces were deployed to the supermarket as authorities sought to secure the release of the hostages.
Images circulating on social media appeared to show people kneeling inside the supermarket with their hands bound. The images could not be independently verified.

blocks.caption: Security forces in Cartagena's La Castellana neighborhood during the hostage crisisImage: Anadolu/IMAGO

blocks.text: Supermarket employees were among those believed to have been taken hostage.
"My son is there," Jacob Perez, the father of one of the workers, told news agency AFP during the standoff.
"He didn't leave work and he's not answering his phone. I think they took it from him," he said.
The supermarket chain said it was following the guidance of the authorities.
"For Grupo Exito, protecting the people's lives and safety is our priority," the company said in a statement.

blocks.caption: A navy helicopter flies over the supermarket in Cartagena during the hostage crisisImage: Alexander Urzola Cuadrado/REUTERS

blocks.text: The incident also temporarily disrupted air traffic in Cartagena, a Caribbean port known for its colonial walled old town, beach resorts and cruise ship tourism.
Arrivals at the city's Rafael Nunez airport were suspended for around 45 minutes in connection with the security operation.
What did Colombia's president say about the hostage crisis?
De la Espriella traveled to Cartagena on Tuesday, where he met commanders from a specialist anti-kidnapping and anti-extortion unit.
The president, who appeared in military fatigues, had previously expressed confidence that the captives would be freed.

blocks.caption: Colombian President Abelardo de la Espriella visited Villavicencio following a car bombing before traveling to CartagenaImage: Alejandro Avendano/AP Photo/picture alliance

blocks.text: "This is going to turn out well for the hostages," he said before arriving in Cartagena. "I'm not so sure it's going to turn out so well for the criminals."
De la Espriella ruled out the involvement of guerrilla or paramilitary groups in the incident.

Local media reported that the hostage-takers had made financial demands and requested safe passage to Barranquilla, another city on Colombia's Caribbean coast. Those reports could not be independently verified.
What is the security situation in Colombia?
Security has deteriorated across much of Colombia despite the tough rhetoric of its right-wing president, who took office in August.
On Monday, a car bombing in the central Colombian city of Villavicencio wounded 25 people and caused extensive damage.

blocks.caption: A destroyed car following a bombing in Villavicencio that wounded 25 people on MondayImage: Mario Toro/AFP

blocks.text: The government blamed the attack on a faction of the former Revolutionary Armed Forces of Colombia (FARC) rebels that rejects a 2016 peace agreement.
De la Espriella had visited Villavicencio following the bombing before traveling to Cartagena.
According to a Defense Ministry document shared with AFP, armed groups carried out 358 drone attacks between January and November — an average of more than one attack per day.

articles.title: IVF, elective abortion, gender-affirming care and VAD to cease under Catholic ownership of private hospitals
articles.summary:
ACCC approves Calvary’s takeover of 14 hospitals around Australia, with critics concerned move will add to pressures on public health system

  • Get our

blocks.text: Advocates say access to voluntary assisted dying, IVF, elective abortions and gender-affirming care is under threat after the competition watchdog approved the takeover of 14 private hospitals by a Catholic healthcare provider.

The Australian Competition and Consumer Commission (ACCC) announced on Wednesday it had approved the takeover of the private hospitals by not-for-profit Catholic healthcare operator Calvary from collapsed provider Healthscope.
In a statement on Wednesday, Calvary welcomed the ACCC’s decision.

A spokesperson for the provider confirmed that under the proposed acquisition, reproductive services including IVF, elective abortions, voluntary assisted dying (VAD) and gender reassignment procedures would cease at any hospitals currently offering those services.
The acquisition, for which a date is not yet confirmed, is still dependent on the issuing of hospital licences by state governments.

Ahead of the ACCC’s announcement on Wednesday, the New South Wales health minister, Ryan Park, announced the state government would step in to support access to IVF at two of the hospitals, John Hunter and Newcastle private hospital, through theatre access at the publicly run John Hunter hospital.
Park said “the vast majority of [other] services will either continue or be available through alternative local providers”.
The 14 hospitals include six in NSW, four in Victoria, two in Brisbane, and one each in the Northern Territory and South Australia. They include rehabilitation clinics as well as private hospitals.
The ACCC has already approved Calvary’s acquisition of Hobart private hospital, with the provider assuming responsibility next month. It took over Holmesglen private hospital in Melbourne last month.

The regulator’s assessment was limited to examining the acquisition’s competition impacts, finding there was “no real likelihood of any operator other than Calvary buying the 14 hospitals”, which were unlikely to remain open otherwise.
But it acknowledged the concerns raised by medical practitioners and community members “that some services would no longer be provided if the acquisition went ahead”.
‘Pay more and wait longer’

As a Catholic healthcare provider, Calvary says it is guided by Catholic Health Australia’s code of ethics. The guidelines say any action or omission that “causes death with the purpose of eliminating all suffering” is not permissible.
The provider has said it will work with clinicians to provide pathways for treatments no longer offered under the acquisition.

Dr Linda Swan, the CEO of charity Go Gentle Australia, described the ACCC’s decision as “disappointing but not unexpected”, saying the organisation was “deeply concerned that Calvary’s acquisitions will reduce choice for dying people”.
after newsletter promotion
“This is not as simple as Calvary wants us to believe. Relocating seriously unwell patients at the end of life is not straightforward and can cause considerable distress and trauma.
“At the same time, the public hospital system is facing ongoing bed shortages. Redirecting more patients into that environment will inevitably increase those pressures.”

The NSW Greens health spokesperson, Amanda Cohn, said the state government had added “insult to injury” by allowing Calvary to continue to operate the troubled public-private partnership at Calvary Mater hospital in Newcastle.

Cohn, who chaired a parliamentary inquiry into the hospital, said patients receiving cancer care or end-of-life care at the hospital had already had to be transferred to Newcastle private to be able to access voluntary assisted dying.
“Where will these patients go, now that this is not an option?” she said.

Dr Nisha Khot, the president of the Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Obstetricians and Gynaecologists (Ranzcog), said the acquisition could put “more pressure on the public healthcare system in the places where Calvary is the only private option”.
“Women who are on a public waitlist, for example, for gynecological surgery, will not get their gynecological surgery because instead somebody who’s having IVF is being prioritised.”
Endocrinologist Prof Ada Cheung, the head of the Trans Health Research Group, said state governments needed to step in to guarantee all forms of care.

“Gender-affirming surgery is mainly delivered privately at significant cost to patients, and public access is very limited across Australia. When options are this scarce, losing any of them means people travel further, pay more and wait longer.”
