articles.title: BCDA commits to no Pax Silica evictions until funds, rights secured
articles.summary: The Bases Conversion and Development Authority has told senators it would not displace residents, clear farmland, or relocate communities for the US-backed Pax Silica hub in Tarlac until funds are…

blocks.text: November 25, 2026 | 1:13pm

MANILA, Philippines — The Bases Conversion and Development Authority has told senators it would not displace residents, clear farmland, or relocate communities for the US-backed Pax Silica hub in Tarlac until funds are secured and residents' rights are respected.

This commitment — made amid mounting criticism of the lack of transparency on the aims and design of the hub, as well as harassment of its critics — was delivered through Sen. Bam Aquino, sponsor of the BCDA's proposed 2027 budget, during plenary debate of the proposed spending plan late Tuesday, November 24.
The BCDA was asked by Sen. Imee Marcos on which agency would fund the relocation of the Aeta and farming families living on the 1,620-hectare planned manufacturing hub in Capas town.
Aquino, relaying the BCDA's answer, said the agency had no estimate yet of what compensation would cost but that future investors in the zone would shoulder the cost.
During plenary debates on the budget, agencies can only answer questions through their designated sponsor on the floor.

"So the BCDA categorically commits that no resident will be displaced, no agricultural land will be cleared, and no community be relocated [until] funds are secured and their rights are acknowledged and respected," Marcos said.
"Yes, there's a commitment," Aquino said.
The Philippines joined Pax Silica, an initiative by the US government to secure supply chains for semiconductors, artificial intelligence and critical minerals and reduce reliance on China, in April.
The government has since set aside a 1,620-hectare "Economic Security Zone" inside New Clark City, on state land administered by the BCDA, which now calls it the Clark Advanced Manufacturing Park.
The plan has met opposition from the Aeta Hungey of Sitio Sapang Kawayan, who have sought recognition of their ancestral domain since 1994, and from farmers in neighboring Barangay O'Donnell.

Rights watchdog Human Rights Watch estimates the hub would displace hundreds of people and that available information indicated the BCDA had not obtained the community's free, prior and informed consent.
Who pays

The BCDA's proposed 2027 budget does not set aside specific funds for the Pax Silica site. However, upon questioning by Sen. Imee Marcos, it confirmed that it may use its corporate funds as "financial assistance" for those that may be displaced.
Aquino, relaying BCDA's answer, said there is "P322 million allocated for financial assistance... This is not particularly in the areas affected by Pax Silica. This is in all BCDA areas."
"But if ever there would be assistance to the families there, it would be coming from this budget... It's in their corporate funds," Aquino said.

Asked whether the BCDA had estimated what it would cost to compensate families for the loss of homes, farmland, crops and livelihoods, and whether P322 million would be enough, Aquino said there was no estimate yet.

However, it would ultimately be the private firms setting up shop, or the "locators," who have to shoulder the cost of transferring residents to a new location and compensating them for any loss of livelihood and income.
It is the locators who would fund the financial support programs, while the BCDA would handle consultations and "social preparation," Aquino said.

This did not sit well with Marcos, who questioned whether this amounted to leaving residents' welfare to private companies. "Eh kung 'yung commercial entity lang ang papasok, sinong lalaban para sa kanila?" she asked. (If only a commercial entity comes in, who will fight for them?)
Aquino said the BCDA would handle residents' concerns while investors paid for the physical development of the site.
Changing numbers of affected. Senators have also flagged the changing numbers of how many actual residents would be affected by the industrial zone.
Aquino said the BCDA's official figure now stood at 198 families, down from close to 400 cited at a Senate hearing in August, while the latest reports place it nearer 1,000.
He said an independent body such as the Department of Social Welfare and Development or the National Commission on Indigenous Peoples (NCIP) should help identify who would be affected.
Quitclaims and relocation
Marcos also told BCDA that senators have received reports from residents who notices to vacate and had been asked to sign quitclaims and waivers for the development of the hub.
Aquino said the BCDA denied asking individuals to sign a quitclaim and was still in talks with affected residents. Marcos said the evidence should be taken up at another hearing.
Human Rights Watch reported this month that farmers in Sitio Binyayan had been offered about P300,000 per hectare and given 10 to 30 days to respond.

Marcos also cited estimates that the hub would need 3 gigawatts of electricity, about 16 percent of Luzon grid capacity, a figure the BCDA itself has used. Aquino said the BCDA acknowledged the figure but planned to generate power on site rather than draw from the grid.
"No power plants are made in two years. Everything takes about five years," Aquino said, adding that this meant investors would likely not locate in the zone for about five years.
Shifting plans

Aquino, though sponsoring the budget, himself criticized the agency's changing descriptions of the project. "Nagsimula 'yan with data center, marami hong umalma... And then suddenly in the hearing wala nang data center. Naging manufacturing pero hindi rin malinaw kung anong klase," he said. (It started as a data center and many objected to that... Then suddenly at the hearing there was no data center. It became manufacturing, but it was not clear what kind.)
"It is important that things are clear to the public and not just to those directly involved, but to all of us. What exactly are we getting ourselves into?" Aquino said in mixed English and Filipino.
"It should be clear to us what the agreements and negotiations entail, and we need to understand exactly what we are entering into here with the United States," he added.
Marcos called for a second Senate hearing on the project and said a follow-up to the first inquiry was long overdue.
The Senate voted in September to constitute itself as a committee of the whole, presided over by Senate President Sherwin Gatchalian, to take up the resolutions filed on Pax Silica.

articles.title: Supreme Court should have ruled on legality of Duterte's ICC arrest — Leonen
articles.summary: In his concurring and dissenting opinion on the ruling, while Leonen agreed to dismiss the petition due to its mootness, he pointed out that the High Court missed an opportunity to establish clear…

blocks.text: November 25, 2026 | 1:03pm

MANILA, Philippines — The Supreme Court should have ruled on the habeas corpus petition filed by former President Rodrigo Duterte challenging his arrest and transfer to the International Criminal Court, Supreme Court Associate Justice Marvic Leonen said.

In his 58-page concurring and dissenting opinion on the ruling, Leonen agreed to dismiss the petition on the ground of mootness but pointed out that the high court missed an opportunity to establish clear guidelines on how international arrest warrants must be executed under the Constitution.

“Summary or extrajudicial killings sponsored by an administration of government are consequential. They impact not only our country but the international community as well. We should take judicial notice that, when sponsored by an administration of government with widespread consequences, its principal perpetrators can be many, and thus arrest and surrender to the International Criminal Court is capable of repetition. That the person of an accused will be surrendered to an International Criminal Court in The Hague means it can evade our review. It can evade review, especially when done in the manner done to the Petitioner in this case. Thus, I cannot agree that we dismiss the Petition by simply declaring that it is moot. That may be politically expedient. That approach tends to undermine our legitimacy as the Court of last resort if we do not provide the clearest guidelines for the bench and bar and, by implication, our law enforcement agencies on the application of the protection of human rights in our laws and the Rome Statute as read through our Constitution.”

The consolidated petitions for a writ of habeas corpus—filed by Duterte’s children, Davao City Mayor Sebastian Duterte, Veronica and Rep. Paolo Duterte (Davao City 1st District)—challenged the legality of the former president's arrest and subsequent transfer to The Hague.

The majority of the Supreme Court justices dismissed the petitions as moot, given that the former president is already in the physical custody of the ICC, which has the competence to determine its own jurisdiction.
Leonen, however, warned that simply declaring the petitions moot is a "politically expedient" cop-out that undermines the Supreme Court's legitimacy as the court of last resort.

“The constitutional issues raised in the present Petitions are grave and serious and capable of repetition, yet evading review. This case cannot simply be dismissed on the ground of mootness, even if doing so may be the politically expedient resolution,” Leonen said.

“As the Court of last resort, we must not shirk our duty of providing the clearest guidelines for the bench and the bar and, by implication, our law enforcement agencies. That is the resolution that would best safeguard and operationalize the human rights provisions under the Rome Statute, which are read through our Constitution,” he added.

Because the former president’s alleged co-perpetrators remain at large in the Philippines and could face similar sudden arrests and transfers, Leonen insisted that the Supreme Court must issue authoritative guidelines to govern future cases.

“It will shape how our trial courts treat the next person arrested for surrender to an international tribunal, and how lawyers advise the officers who make the arrest. If we do the expedient thing and leave the question unanswered, we teach the bench and the bar that comfort, convenience, and the political agenda of the day may decide what due process requires. That would be a lesson in a lesser version of our profession, and this Court should not be the one to teach it,” Leonen said.

"While upholding the International Criminal Court's jurisdiction to prosecute his offenses, this Court should also have made clear that the manner of his surrender was inconsistent with our own legal order," he added.
Hasty arrest
Duterte was taken into custody at the Ninoy Aquino International Airport on March 11, 2025, based on an ICC arrest warrant and an Interpol diffusion request.
Within hours, he was placed on a plane destined for The Hague, with custody officially transferred to the ICC by the following day.
Leonen pointed out that this rapid-fire transfer completely bypassed local judicial systems, violating Duterte's right to due process under the Constitution.

Under Article 59 of the Rome Statute—which remains binding on the Philippines for acts committed prior to its 2019 withdrawal—any person arrested under an ICC warrant must be brought "promptly" before a competent judicial authority in the custodial state.

Leonen argued that Philippine authorities were duty-bound to present Duterte before a local court to verify his identity, ensure proper process was followed, and confirm his constitutional rights were respected.

“Moreover, because he was arrested and surrendered on the same day (March 11, 2025), former President Duterte was also completely deprived of his lawful opportunity under Article 59(3) of the Rome Statute to apply to any competent domestic authority for interim release pending surrender to the International Criminal Court,” Leonen said.

“The principal constitutional defect lay not in the absence of a fresh determination of probable cause that question belonged to the issuing international court or tribunal but in the total absence of any judicial review: former President Duterte was taken and flown to The Hague within hours, without any judicial imprimatur sought by his captors. That omission was a real violation of his right to be free from seizure except through judicial process,” he added.
Protecting the powerless
Leonen acknowledged that Duterte is widely despised by many for the alleged summary executions committed during his administration's "war on drugs.”
He noted that denying Duterte due process might "win wide acclaim" and satisfy those seeking accountability.
However, Leonen cautioned that the Supreme Court cannot decide cases based on political comfort or visceral temptation.
He stressed that the legal procedures bypassed in Duterte's arrest are the same safeguards that protect ordinary citizens.
"The procedure that protects a former president is the same procedure that protects the farmer taken at night and the young father picked up in an operation in a crowded barangay," Leonen said.
"Whatever we refuse to the powerful, we will soon be unable to guarantee to the powerless,” he added.

articles.title: In charts: how power could shift in Europe’s big year of elections
articles.summary:
More than half of EU voters will go to the polls in the next 12 months, with the far right targeting significant gains. We set out the political landscape and trends

Over the coming 12…
articles.byline: Jon Henley, Jakub Krupa and Seán Clarke

blocks.text: Over the coming 12 months, more than half of the EU’s electorate will go to the polls in elections that could change the direction of the continent, with attention focused on voters in four of the bloc’s five biggest states.

In Spain, France and Poland, elections could bring the far right into government. Italy’s far-right prime minister looks likely to remain in power, but is under pressure from a challenger even more to the right.

While few of Europe’s far-right parties want to leave the EU, they still see the bloc as a top-down project that undermines national sovereignty and are bent on transforming it into something far looser.

The graphics below map the main political parties in each country along two ideological axes – economic left-right and libertarian-authoritarian – using data from researchers at the Chapel Hill Expert Survey. Polling averages then show how the race is developing.
Spain
Parliamentary election on 29 November
Spain will head to the polls on Sunday to vote in a sixth general election in 11 years. The snap election could end eight years of socialist-led rule and bring a far-right party into government.

Since the restoration of democracy in Spain in 1977, every prime minister has come from one of three parties: the now-disbanded Union of the Democratic Centre, a very broad centrist alliance from the time of the transition; the centre-right People’s party (PP); and the centre-left Socialist Workers’ party (PSOE).

Often the ruling party has needed the support of smaller parties, sometimes regional groups. But, as elsewhere in Europe, the traditional centre-right and centre-left parties are being challenged by populists further to the left and right.

Since 2023, Pedro Sánchez has been in government with the support of Sumar, which sits ideologically to the left of his PSOE party. But polling suggests that PSOE and Sumar’s latest incarnation, Broad Front, will together fail to muster a majority in parliament.

That leaves the door partly open to the PP, led by Alberto Núñez Feijóo, but he too will need support, and just as Sánchez looked to his left, it is thought Feijóo will look to his right, bringing the far-right Vox of Santiago Abascal into government. Abascal this week told a rally that “remigration sounds to me like heavenly music”.
France
Presidential election on 18 April and 2 May 2027

The sitting president, Emmanuel Macron, has served the maximum two terms and will be an onlooker in spring’s election. If, as usual, no candidate wins 50% in the first round of voting, the two leading candidates go into a runoff two weeks later. Polling suggests that Marine Le Pen, the leader of the far-right Rassemblement National (the National Rally) will be one of those two, for the third time.

But unlike on previous occasions, there is no obvious centrist candidate to challenge her in the second round. The president’s heirs apparent – Gabriel Attal of Macron’s Renaissance party and Édouard Philippe of coalition partners Horizons – are splitting the centrist vote. Both were prime ministers under Macron – but then so were five other politicians.

Raphaël Glucksmann, a former Socialist who left to found his own party, is nonetheless the Socialist and centre-left candidate. He is outflanked on the left by Jean-Luc Mélenchon, who seems most likely to face Le Pen in the second round. In the contest between the far left and far right, the polls suggest Le Pen will be the victor.
Poland
Parliamentary election 11 November 2027

For 20 years, the prime ministers of Poland have come from one of two parties, the hard-right Law and Justice (PiS) party, or the Civic Platform – now Civic Coalition (KO) – of Donald Tusk, a centrist and relatively libertarian party which is in government. The two parties’ starkly opposing ideas and practices have led to constitutional crisis, not least because the PiS holds the presidency.

Although polling shows support for the PiS faltering, Tusk can take little comfort – much of that support seems to be flowing toward parties even farther to the right; Konfederacja (Confederation), a libertarian nationalist far-right coalition, and their former allies, the Confederation of the Polish Crown (KKP). KKP was last assessed by Chapel Hill researchers in 2024 as part of Konfederacja, but the party is significantly further to the authoritarian right. It is also the only party that advocates Poland’s withdrawal from the EU and faces regular criticism for pro-Russian positions on foreign policy.

Even worse for Tusk, two of his three coalition partners – the centre-right Polska 2050 and the conservative agrarian PSL – are at risk of polling below the 5% threshold needed to enter parliament. Their success or failure in clearing that threshold could play a major role in deciding the election.
Italy
Parliamentary election due by 22 December 2027

The last of the big four is Italy, where the far right has been in power since 2022. Giorgia Meloni’s Fratelli d’Italia (Brothers of Italy) party has been in a rightwing coalition with Lega (League) and the relatively centrist Forza Italia.
Meloni is odds on to remain prime minister after the election, according to the Polymarket betting site. But she is under pressure, perhaps surprisingly, from the right.

Roberto Vannacci, a retired general, has started a far-right party, Futuro Nazionale (National Future), and is polling at least as well as Meloni’s coalition partners. Vannacci’s party is too new to have been assessed by Chapel Hill researchers, but given that his stated reason for leaving Lega was that it was insufficiently rightwing, it is very probably in the upper right quadrant of the chart.

articles.title: ‘They don’t believe in freedom’: Yemenis plan their escape as Houthis advance on Aden
articles.summary:
With Iran’s proxy fighters encircling the temporary capital, residents and NGOs prepare to evacuate

Hussein fled his home six years ago after it fell under Houthi control, moving as far…
articles.byline: A reporter in southern Yemen and William Christou in Beirut

blocks.text: Hussein fled his home six years ago after it fell under Houthi control, moving as far south as he could to the port city of Aden, where there was a measure of safety.
The Saudi-backed Yemeni government had made the city its temporary capital; the hundreds of kilometres between it and the Houthis were well fortified.

Today, Hussein is once again considering the painful decision of leaving home. In September, the Iran-aligned Houthis swept aside Yemeni government forces, and now have set their sights on Aden. Houthi fighters are amassing to the north and east of the city, and have begun encircling the government-controlled territory.

blocks.caption: People displaced by war on the Red Sea coastline receive aid near Aden, Yemen. Photograph: Reuters

blocks.text: “I fled my home in Sana’a and came here. I don’t think the Houthis plan to take over Aden right now, but if they get closer, I will have no choice but to flee again to Marib or Hadhramaut,” said Hussein, who was speaking under a pseudonym.

Hussein works as a schoolteacher and was formerly a member of the Islah party, an Islamist political party aligned with Saudi Arabia that is in opposition to the Houthi movement. He fears that if the Houthis take control of Aden he could face persecution for his former affiliation.
“The Houthis don’t believe in freedom, they just want to hear one voice, the one they like,” he said.

Hussein is one of many residents and organisations nervously watching the Houthi advance. The militia is still about 50 miles (80km) north of Aden, but local people fear government forces may not be able to resist another Houthi assault, having seen the dramatic collapse of government forces and allied militias in September.

blocks.caption: Houthi forces take over from Dhubab to Bab el-Mandeb, Taiz governorate, Yemen, after Saudi-backed forces withdraw from the area, 16 November 2026. Photograph: Houthi Military Media/Reuters

blocks.text: Aden has been the seat of the Saudi-backed government of Yemen since 2015. If the Houthis took the city, it would be a huge blow for the government, and a massive failure for the Saudi-led coalition which has for years fought against the Houthis.
The 12-year-long civil war would tilt dramatically in the Houthis’ favour and be a boon for Iran, which has long invested military and political support in the insurgent movement.

The Yemeni government has pulled back many of its fighters to help defend Aden and the surrounding areas, announcing last week that fighters were redeployed from areas along the south-western coast towards the port city.

Saudi Arabia has tried to halt the Houthi advance with a renewed bombing campaign, carrying out hundreds of airstrikes in Yemen since September, killing and wounding 822 civilians, including 181 children, according to statistics from the independent Yemen Data Project.
Houthi authorities have alleged that Saudi Arabia has carried out 5,500 air and missile attacks since July.

blocks.caption: A rescuer walks through the debris of a destroyed building belonging to Yemen’s Public Telecommunications Corporation following a Saudi strike in the port city of Hodeida. Photograph: AFP/Getty Images

blocks.text: The Houthis have not announced any intention to take Aden, but have instead been amassing troops north of Kirish, and in al-Bayda, areas which, if taken, would cut off the northern and eastern roads to Aden.
“The buildups in al-Bayda could threaten Aden’s eastern road links through Abyan and Saudi supply lines into the city,” said Mohammed al-Basha, the founder of the US-based risk advisory Basha Report.

“The Houthis appear to be testing how well Aden’s defences will hold. If they collapse, the Houthis could try to seize the city. If government forces hold, the Houthis could try to lay siege to it,” al-Basha added.

blocks.caption: Members of the National Security Forces at a checkpoint as security is tightened in Aden. Photograph: Reuters

blocks.text: Houthi forces have begun striking Aden and its surrounding areas, rupturing the relative safety the city has offered for years. Residents have watched anxiously as explosions grow nearer, and displaced people from surrounding areas have started to arrive in greater numbers.
“Since last week, we’ve started following the news every hour. When I get busy, I tell my daughter to follow it and update me,” said Rami, a resident of Aden who spoke under a pseudonym.

The 53-year-old bitterly recalled his experience during the four-month battle for Aden in 2015, when he was stuck in the crossfire between the Houthis and Yemeni government forces. He, like other people in Aden, is trying to make his own calculation of when, or if, the Houthis will arrive.
International organisations are also making contingency plans in case of a Houthi takeover of the city.

blocks.caption: A displaced woman carries an aid box at the al-Fardous displacement camp in Ras Imran, on the outskirts of Aden. Photograph: Abdulnasser Alseddik/AP

blocks.text: “We were informed by management that they are issuing termination notices to all staff this week. If the Houthis don’t reach Aden, they will continue operations and renew our contracts; otherwise this is the end of the road,” an aid worker with an international NGO said.
Already, several NGOs were forced to shut down in the city of Taiz after sweeping Houthi gains.

Not all NGOs would leave in the case of a Houthi takeover, but some are unable to work in Houthi-controlled areas either due to fears for the safety of aid workers, or because the US Treasury designated the Houthis a foreign terrorist organisation in 2025.
Yemen has for years faced a severe humanitarian crisis, with about 18.7 million people facing acute food insecurity.

blocks.caption: Displaced Yemenis from the west coast wait to receive medical care at Prince Mohammed bin Salman hospital in Aden. Photograph: Abdulnasser Alseddik/AP

blocks.text: Fighting has only exacerbated conditions, severing transport routes, pushing up the prices of goods and worsening the country’s displacement crisis – including more than 350,000 people displaced since August.

“I earn daily wages, and when there is no work, my six family members don’t get enough food,” said Ahmed, a restaurant worker in his 50s. “I don’t care about politics or wars, and I’m not involved in any of it. I’m just like millions of Yemenis struggling to provide basic necessities for their families.”
For many of Aden’s residents, the prospect of a Houthi takeover has shattered the sense of safety that they sought by coming to the government stronghold in the first place.

“I’m not stocking up on food because I won’t stay in Aden and wait for the battles to reach the city. It isn’t only me; my family is also ready to flee at any time … staying at home won’t be safe and we might get trapped,” Rami said.

blocks.text: Here are the biggest headlines from India on Wednesday, November 25:
November 25, 2026
US set to unveil new tariffs after probe on excess factory capacity

India could be one of the 16 countries facing fresh and imminent US tariffs with the Trump administration set to release the findings of a probe aimed at countering alleged excess industrial capacities, Reuters reported citing three people with knowledge of the matter.
The results of the investigation are likely to be released over the course of the day, followed by new import duties on a wide range of goods if the probe find India guilty of excess capacity.
It remains unclear what tariff rates would be proposed but one of the sources told the news agency that they would be specifically tailored to each country.
That said, the US is likely to honor capped tariff rates agreed on in finalized US trade deals with partner countries.
A report by the Wall Street Journal said that India could face higher US tariffs than economies like Japan or the European Union.
Where are US tariffs on India?

The US introduced 25% reciprocal tariffs in 2025 on India, under US President Donald Trump's second term. The rate was later lowered to 18% with Washington and New Delhi agreeing to an interim trade framework while a more comprehensive trade agreement would be worked on. Leaders from both nations have since said the first tranche of a trade agreement was "close," but a deal remains elusive.

Meanwhile in July 2026, the United States Trade Representative (USTR), which carries out trade-related investigations, imposed an additional 10% tariffs on India and other countries after a probe on traded goods made using forced labor.

articles.title: Marcos vows sustained support vs stunting under Alagang Pinas Summit
articles.summary: President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. vowed Wednesday to sustain government programs aimed at protecting pregnant mothers and children up to two years old from stunting, as the Philippine Multisectoral…

blocks.text: Published November 25, 2026 12:01pm

President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. vowed Wednesday to sustain government programs aimed at protecting pregnant mothers and children up to two years old from stunting, as the Philippine Multisectoral Nutrition Project (PMNP) concludes its four-year project.

“Sa pamamagitan ng Alagang Pinas Summit, ang mga serbisyon na simulan sa ilalim ng PMNP ay magpapatuloy upang ang bawat batang nangangailangan ng tulong sa nutrisyon ay makakatanggap ng angkop at sapat na pangangalaga,” Marcos said during his speech in Clark, Pampanga.
(Through the Alagang Pinas Summit, the services initiated under the PMNP will continue to ensure that every child in need of nutritional support receives appropriate and adequate care.)

The PMNP is an initiative between the Department of Health (DOH), the World Bank, and the United Nations Children's Fund (UNICEF) that aims to reduce child stunting and malnutrition by boosting access to nutrition to pregnant mothers and infants during the critical first 1,000 days.
The summit also marks the culmination of the four-year PMNP with the theme “Alagang Pinas Tungo sa Mas Malusog na Bukas: Sustained First 1,000 Days (F1KD) Convergence.”
According to Marcos, PMNP has reached 6.17 million beneficiaries in 235 participating municipalities as of Sept. 30, 2026.
Meanwhile, around 549,000 children under five benefited from the program, while 134 participating municipalities recorded significant reductions in stunting after two years.
Marcos also said the government is strengthening local implementation capacity while acknowledging existing limitations and gaps that need to be addressed.
According to DOH, the rate among children under 2 years old in the Philippines declined from 22.5% in 2023 to 21.1% in 2025.

Health Secretary Edwin Mercado had said eight out of 10 children aged 2 years old and below have adequate height for their age. The stunting rate slightly decreased from 22.5% in 2023 to 21.1% in 2025.

However, he said it is still far from the Millennium Development targets under the Philippine Plan of Action for Nutrition (PPAN) 2023–2028, which aims to reduce the stunting rate among children under 5 years old to 17.9% or lower by 2028.
Protect funding
In her speech, UNICEF representative in the Philippines Kyungsun Kim called for the protection of funds against stunting.
“Protect funding for nutrition year after year. Prioritizing interventions during the first 1,000 days matters,” Kim said, underscoring the importance of regularly measuring results.
“Projects have timelines, but a child's right to good health and nutrition does not,” she said.
“Keep nutrition at the heart of development plans. Make sure services reach those who need them most,” she added.
Meanwhile, Mercado pointed out the factors that need to be considered in addressing malnutrition and stunting.

“The reality is no single agency can solve malnutrition alone. It is never just a clinical issue, it is tied to clean water, early childhood care, food security, social protection, and strong local governance,” he said during the summit. — RSJ, GMA News

articles.title: Martin Romualdez appeals 90-day suspension, says plunder allegations unclear
articles.summary: Leyte Rep. Martin Romualdez has appealed the 90-day suspension imposed by the Sandiganbayan, saying it is premature amid the prosecution"s unclear P7.4 billion plunder charge.

blocks.text: Published November 25, 2026 12:01pm
Leyte Rep. Martin Romualdez has appealed the 90-day suspension imposed by the Sandiganbayan, saying it is premature amid the prosecution’s unclear P7.4 billion plunder charge.

In his motion for reconsideration, Romualdez said the Sandiganbayan did not rule on his argument that the prosecution did not identify a main plunderer, even if a 2016 Supreme Court ruling on the Arroyo v. People case requires that such should be identified when a case is filed against several individuals.

“With due respect, the [criminal] Information charges accused Romualdez and Co together with receiving the monies “by reason or on account of the respective public offices and positions of Romualdez and Co,” and with “taking undue advantage, on several occasions, of their respective official positions, authorities, relationships, connections, or influence to unjustly enrich themselves.” It does not state which of the two is the main plunderer, either does it state how much of the aggregate of P7.4 billion each of them supposedly amassed,” the former House speaker said in his appeal.

“The Questioned Resolution [imposing a suspension order] reads the Information as alleging that accused Romualdez amassed the ill-gotten wealth. The Information does not allege that accused Romualdez, as distinguished from Co, amassed it. It alleges only that Romualdez and Co enriched “themselves.” This, too, must be resolved before the Information may serve as the basis for preventive suspension,” he added.

Romualdez’s co-accused in the P7.4 billion plunder case include former House appropriations chairperson Zaldy Co of Ako Bicol party-list, Romualdez’s personal assistant Joselyn Tragua Sereño, and Felicito Cristobal Guevarra, president of Samchan Foreign Exchange Corporation.

“Accused Romualdez is not identified as having personally received any sum on any of the 15 occasions alleged. Neither does the [criminal information distinguish supposed receipts by an approximate date, amount, or identified transaction. A bare statement of 15 occasions, an aggregate amount, and delivery locations, do not sufficiently identify the component criminal transactions comprising the alleged series,” the lawmaker said.

Romualdez said that while the issue on whether he committed the alleged acts is a matter for trial, whether those acts have been sufficiently alleged is another question that needs to be resolved first.
“The latter must be resolved before the [criminal] information may serve as the basis for preventive suspension,” he said. —AOL, GMA News

articles.title: Kilmar Ábrego García leaving US for Spain, ending Trump deportation battle
articles.summary: His deportation to El Salvador and return to the US became a flash point in the debate over President Donald Trump's immigration agenda.

blocks.text: Kilmar Ábrego García, whose deportation last year to El Salvador sparked a bitter deportation battle, is leaving the US for Spain.
He is set to take a commercial flight to the country on Tuesday, according to CBS News, the BBC's US partner.

After the government admitted it had wrongfully sent Ábrego García to his home country, he was returned to the US to face human trafficking charges, which were later dropped. The administration then continued its attempts to send him to other countries, including Uganda and Ghana.
His deportation and return became a flashpoint in the debate over President Donald Trump's immigration agenda.
Ábrego García, who is married to a US citizen and lived in Maryland, came to the US illegally from El Salvador as a teenager.
Senator Chris Van Hollen, a Democrat from Maryland, visited Ábrego García while he was in the notorious Cecot prison in El Salvador in 2025 and advocated for his release.

"A year and a half ago, the Trump Administration wanted to leave Kilmar Ábrego García to rot in a Salvadoran gulag," Van Hollen said in a statement on Tuesday. "Today, Kilmar is travelling to a country of his choice, a free man - unharmed and with dignity."
The BBC has contacted Ábrego García's lawyers and the US Department of Homeland Security for comment.

Ábrego García was arrested in 2019 alongside three other men and detained by federal immigration authorities. A judge granted him protection from deportation to El Salvador at the time, citing the risk of persecution by a gang there.

In March 2025, the Trump administration deported him to El Salvador, where he was held in Cecot, a prison known for its harsh conditions. The US Supreme Court then ordered the government to facilitate his return.

The administration admitted that he was deported in error and brought him back to the US where he was set to face human trafficking charges. A federal judge dismissed the case, saying Ábrego García had been charged for political reasons.
For months, he was locked in a battle over deportation with the government.
Ábrego García had repeatedly said he would be willing to be deported to Costa Rica, and the Costa Rican government had agreed to accept him as a refugee and provide him with legal status.
After reports emerged that the administration was considering sending him to Uganda, a judge barred the government from deporting Ábrego García to a third country.
At one point the Trump administration requested that the judge lift the order so that Ábrego García could be deported to Liberia, CBS reported.

articles.title: Watchdog hits Cayetano's proposal for Filipinos to pay P170,000 each in debt
articles.summary: A civil society watchdog said that Sen. Alan Peter Cayetano's suggestion to have Filipinos voluntarily contribute toward repaying the country's debt was "out of touch and insensitive" amid soaring…

blocks.text: November 25, 2026 | 11:35am
Senate President Alan Peter Cayetano holds a press briefing at the Senate on Wednesday, claiming he did not know on Sunday night, May 10, whether Sen. Bato dela Rosa would come to the Senate.
The STAR / Ryan Baldemor

MANILA, Philippines — A civil society watchdog said that Sen. Alan Peter Cayetano's suggestion to have Filipinos voluntarily contribute toward repaying the country's debt was "out of touch and insensitive" amid soaring inflation and the rising cost of living.

During the Senate budget deliberations on Monday, November 23, Cayetano put forward the idea of developing a mechanism to allow each citizen to pay their share of the country's P19.66 trillion debt, equivalent to around P170,000 each.

People's Budget Coalition spokesperson AJ Montesa told DZBB on Wednesday, November 25, that the organization was surprised to hear the suggestion during the budget hearing on Monday, saying that many Filipinos were unlikely to have such an amount at their disposal.
The spokesperson also said that referring only to debt-per-capita ratios was a misleading way of framing debt.

The debt-per-capita measure divides a country's debt by its population and was Cayetano's basis for the P170,598.03 figure mentioned during the hearing. The ratio notably takes into consideration volatile economic factors like inflation and foreign currency exchange rates, recent movements in both of which have sparked fears of stagflation.
Headline inflation rose to 7.8% in October 2026. The peso-dollar exchange rate, meanwhile, has lingered near the P64:$1 mark, opening at P63.67 to the dollar on Wednesday.

Evaluating how a country's debt compares to its gross domestic product, or the value of finished goods and services rendered within its borders, was a better way to determine a country's ability to pay, Montesa said.
President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. originally aimed to lower the country's debt-to-GDP ratio from 60% to 51% by the end of his term. The ratio, however, hit a 22-year high of 66.99% in November 2026.

"Bumaliktad pa doon sa target natin ang naging achievement ng Marcos administration dahil nga mali ang paggastos natin ng pera. So, lumolobo 'yong utang natin. Hindi napupunta ('yong pera) sa tamang paggastos. 'Yong economy natin, humihina ... Our indicators are very bad," Montesa said.

(Our achievement under the Marcos administration has gone in the opposite direction of our target because we have been spending our money improperly. So, our debt continues to balloon. The money is not being spent properly. Our economy is weakening ... Our indicators are very bad.)

He added that a higher debt-to-GDP ratio could be acceptable if loans are used "correctly" because debt can sometimes be necessary during economic crises. However, reports of slowing economic growth, rising inflation and currency depreciation raise concerns about the country's financial condition.

In addition to record-high inflation and sluggish growth, the Philippines' dollar reserves fell to $98 billion in October 2026, prompting Bangko Sentral ng Pilipinas Governor Eli Remolona Jr. to describe the situation as "scary" during the Senate budget hearing on Tuesday, November 24.
He later said that the $98-billion level was still “a bit safe” because it was equivalent to six months of imports and “three times the country’s short-term debt."

Dollar reserves affect economic factors like inflation by stabilizing a country's currency and promoting price stability, especially for goods purchased in dollars, such as fuel and certain food items. Fuel and food costs were the top contributors to inflation in October.

articles.title: Solomon Islands ends controversial security pact with China for Australian treaty
articles.summary: Solomon Islands leader Matthew Wale said his country would no longer be a point of regional uncertainty.

blocks.text: The Solomon Islands has signed a "historic" treaty with Australia, after reportedly telling China it was ending a controversial security pact signed in 2022.

At a press conference in Canberra on Wednesday, Australian Prime Minister Anthony Albanese and Solomon Islands counterpart Matthew Wale said the new treaty would ensure that Australia was the Pacific nation's "security partner of choice".
In 2022 the Solomon Islands, then under the leadership of now-Opposition Leader Manasseh Sogavare, signed a security and policing pact with Beijing.
There were fears the pact gave China a crucial military and strategic foothold in the Pacific amid a battle for influence in the region with the US.
On Tuesday, Australian media outlets reported that Honiara had told Beijing it would not renew the pact, understood to be expiring in April 2027.
Wale told reporters on Wednesday there were "ongoing discussions" with China but he was "unable to talk about" the pact, because of a non-disclosure agreement.
He said the treaty with Australia provided a reset after several years in which the Solomon Islands had been a point of "uncertainty and doubt in the region".
"Those days are done, gone," Wale said.
Albanese said the treaty would strengthen the two countries' security partnership.
"Backing our Pacific neighbours is an investment in Australia's own security and our own prosperity."
"We'll do that in a way that completely respects Solomon Islands sovereignty and its right to make its own decisions."
On Tuesday China's foreign ministry spokesman, Guo Jiukan, did not confirm or deny that the pact had been terminated.
"There is no element of geopolitical rivalry or bloc confrontation in cooperation between China and Pacific island countries, including the Solomon Islands," Guo said.

The pact was never publicly released, but leaked excerpts revealed it gave China extensive involvement in security and policing including deploying its own officers to the Solomon Islands, and allowed it to establish a quasi military base.
It was a "massive coup" for Beijing, said Lowy Institute Research Fellow, Dr Connor Graham, but its unprecedented scale sparked alarm in the Pacific and the West.
Wednesday's treaty had delivered "an enormous win for Canberra", and "closes the loop" on a series of security deals Canberra signed with Pacific nations in the wake of the Solomons-China pact.
"That [China pact] was the thing that put fear in the hearts of diplomats in Washington and Canberra," he told the BBC.

William Yang, the International Crisis Group's Senior Analyst for North East Asia, said the end of China's "flagship" Pacific deal and the signing of the new treaty also reaffirmed the Pacific's "longstanding consensus-based decision-making model, especially in the security space".

Under the new treaty, the Solomon Islands commits to prior consultation with Australia on critical infrastructure and to ensure any security cooperations are with Pacific Islands Forum members. China is a dialogue partner but not a member of the forum.

Honiara also commits to its sensitive infrastructure remaining "free from militarisation, any form of foreign interference or unauthorised access", and to not permit its territory to be used for any foreign military or security base.

The Solomons will receive support for its free education system and sports programs, improved visa arrangements, and support for the expansion of affordable and renewable energy and infrastructure development.

Earlier this week the ABC reported the package promised more than A$980m (£460.7m, $648,000) in additional funding, citing leaked text messages. The BBC has not independently verified the text messages.

Wale visited Australia to sign the treaty, accompanied by two dozen Solomons MPs. He and Albanese said the size of the delegation demonstrated that the treaty had strong support from the country's parliament, after years of political instability - largely driven by disagreement over the country's relationship with China.

articles.title: The Russian army’s secret death toll – podcast
articles.summary: Vladimir Putin has always kept the number of soldiers killed in Ukraine a secret, but at one point 720 were dying in 24 hours. Pjotr Sauer reports. Send your comments and questions to
articles.byline: Presented by Helen Pidd with Pjotr Sauer; produced by Eli Block, George McDonagh , Alex Atack and Ross Burns; executive producer Homa Khaleeli

blocks.text: Russia has kept the death toll of its soldiers in the Ukraine war a carefully guarded secret. Now documents leaked to the Guardian have revealed its true scale. The Guardian’s Russia affairs correspondent, Pjotr Sauer, tells Helen Pidd what reporters have discovered.

Two groups of hackers accessed Russia’s main statistics database last month and discovered a cache of 11m death certificates that revealed nearly 500,000 Russian losses in Ukraine since 2022. Among these were 1,000 – the equivalent of a whole regiment – who took their own lives.

The documents show how the majority of soldiers come from poorer areas and ethnic minorities, drawn in by high salaries. There are also recruits from abroad and even those lured to Russia by offers of jobs. But for how long can Vladimir Putin keep this shocking death toll from the Russian people?

articles.title: China launches Shenzhou-24 to Tiangong station
articles.summary: A new Chinese crew is on its way to the Tiangong station after a launch that China called a complete success. This includes a Pakistani pilot, who is making a brief visit.

image.caption: A rocket carrying the Shenzhou-24 spacecraft has blasted off to China's Tiangong space station from the Jiuquan Satellite Launch CenterImage: Tingshu Wang/REUTERS

blocks.text: The Shenzhou-24 spacecraft lifted off on a Long March-2F rocket at 8:18 am local time (0018 GMT) from the Jiuquan launch center in the Gobi Desert.
The China Manned Space Agency reported that the capsule separated from the rocket about 10 minutes later and entered orbit, and called the launch a "complete success".
State broadcaster CCTV showed the three crew members leafing through a manual minutes after liftoff and reported that they were in good condition.
What do we know about the crew?

Tang Hongbo is making his third trip to space. CCTV said he will become the first astronaut to board Tiangong three times. Wu Yi is on his first flight, as is Pakistani pilot Muhammad Zeeshan Ali, the first foreigner to fly on a Chinese crewed mission.
"I carry the name of Pakistan on my shoulder, the hopes of 250 million Pakistanis," Ali told a news conference on Tuesday, switching between Urdu, Mandarin and English.
China-Pakistan space ties

The handover on the station will be unusual. Shenzhou-23 commander Zhu Yangzhu will remain on board for a year, while the rest of his crew — Lai Ka-ying, Hong Kong's first astronaut, and Zhang Zhiyuan — return to Earth with Ali.

Zhu's stay is reportedly China's first full-year spell in space. Reuters said it will be the longest single stay by a Chinese astronaut. It has been described as a test of how the human body copes, ahead of planned Moon missions and possibly a journey to Mars.
What is on the agenda?

The crew will carry out more than 90 experiments and technology tests, Xinhua reported. At a news conference on Tuesday, Tang said differences in language, culture and psychology had made teamwork harder, but that both sides' efforts were paying off.
Ali, speaking in Mandarin, told reporters: "It's like my daily training. Day after day, reaching new heights."
China's 2030 target for a crewed Moon landing is unchanged despite the delay to its Chang'e-7 lunar mission. The United States is aiming for 2028.

articles.title: Al Gore buys local, family-owned newspaper in central Tennessee
articles.summary:
Former vice-president, who started his career as a journalist, purchases Carthage Courier in Smith county

Al Gore, who started his career as a journalist, is returning to the industry as a…

blocks.text: Al Gore, who started his career as a journalist, is returning to the industry as a newspaper owner in his Tennessee town.

The Lake family, which has operated the Carthage Courier for five decades, said Tuesday it will sell the paper to the former vice-president in the coming weeks. The weekly paper serves Smith county in central Tennessee, which has roughly 20,000 residents and sits about 55 miles (88km) east of Nashville.

As the beleaguered news industry struggles with newspaper closures and growing news deserts, Gore characterized the purchase as a move that preserves an independent local voice in Carthage and Smith county.

“Having spent my early years as a military reporter in Vietnam and later at the [Nashville] Tennessean, I am a firm believer that a free, independent local press is irreplaceable for the enduring health of our community,” Gore said in a statement.

Terms of the sale weren’t disclosed, and it wasn’t clear how involved Gore, 78, will be in the paper’s operations. His office and the outlet wouldn’t answer questions Tuesday or provide additional details.
The Courier’s announcement omitted Gore’s political résumé, presenting him simply as a local man buying his small town’s paper to keep it locally owned.

Before entering politics, Gore spent six months as a military reporter in the US Army during the Vietnam war. He returned to Tennessee and worked for a few years as an investigative reporter at the Tennessean before running for Congress in 1976.

Gore, a Democrat, represented Tennessee in both chambers of Congress, served as Bill Clinton’s vice-president from 1993 to 2001, and ran for president twice. After losing the 2000 presidential election to George W Bush, he went on to win the Nobel peace prize for his climate activism and an Academy award for the documentary An Inconvenient Truth.
The Courier’s website notes that it covered the early political pursuits of Gore’s father, Albert Gore Sr, who represented the state in the US House and Senate.

Tim Franklin, chair of local news at Northwestern University’s Medill School of Journalism, Media, Integrated Marketing Communications, said Carthage residents may have “some healthy skepticism” about a politician owning the paper.
“But I would be surprised if the Carthage Courier becomes a mouthpiece for the Democratic party,” he said.

Gore is far from the first politician to purchase or own a newspaper. Throughout the 1900s, several senators, governors and even a US president, Warren Harding, had local papers in their business portfolios.

More recently, consumer advocate Ralph Nader, one of Gore’s former political rivals, helped launch a local newspaper in Winsted, Connecticut, in 2023 that was purchased months later by a national media company.

articles.title: Rescue crews search for six people after plane crash off Mississippi coast
articles.summary:
US Coast Guard said crews had so far found the cabin of the plane, a life raft and three life jackets

Rescue crews were searching for six people on board a small plane that crashed Tuesday…

blocks.text: Rescue crews were searching for six people on board a small plane that crashed Tuesday afternoon off the coast of Mississippi.
Crews have so far found three life jackets, a life raft and the cabin of the plane. The plane’s cabin was floating on the water, Juan Ros, a US Coast Guard spokesperson, said.

The plane, a Cessna 210, went down around 3.30pm in the Gulf of Mexico between Pascagoula, Mississippi, and Horn Island, which is part of the Gulf Islands national seashore. There were four adults and two boys, ages eight and 10, on board, authorities said.
The Cessna was en route from New Orleans to Fort Meyers, Florida, according to the flight tracking website FlightAware.
According to the Coast Guard, the plane was descending at a rate of 10,000ft per minute when contact was lost.
The Federal Aviation Administration and the National Transportation Safety Board, which will investigate the crash, said on Tuesday they were aware of it.

articles.title: US jury convicts Huawei of violating sanctions, stealing trade secrets
articles.summary: Huawei was found guilty of 10 out of 12 charges levelled against it. The company said it plans to appeal the verdict.

image.caption: Chinese tech giant Huawei was already banned from selling 5G networking tech in the USImage: Mark Schiefelbein/AP Photo/picture alliance

blocks.text: A US jury convicted Chinese tech giant Huawei on a slew of charges on Tuesday including stealing trade secrets and violating sanctions.
The jury in the Brooklyn federal court found the company guilty on 10 of the 12 criminal counts that it faced, which also included bank fraud and wire fraud.
"For decades, Huawei and three of its subsidiaries conducted their business in the United States on the basis of lies and theft," US Attorney General Todd Blanche said after the verdict.
However, the jury acquitted Huawei on two charges of racketeering and conspiring to obstruct justice.

The verdict is the latest blow to the Chinese tech giant which has for years been banned from selling networking devices to telecom carries in the US and other Western countries. However, its consumer electronics business has continued to grow as its networking business in other countries.
Stolen source code, antenna technology and robot tech
Prosecutors detailed a number of ways Huawei stole trade secrets from competitors in order to undercut them in the market.
In once instance, a Huawei employee slipped into a competitor's booth at a Chicago trade fair in order to photograph circuitboards inside another company's networking divice.
Huawei was also found to have once sold routers containing source code from a rival company.
How the China-US AI arms race is escalating
Prosecutors also said a Huawei employee once removed a robotic arm from a competitor's lab so it could be photographed and measured.
According to court records, the victim companies included Cisco Systems, Motorola Solutions, T-Mobile, Quintel USA and Fujitsu.

"The misappropriated intellectual property included trade secret information and copyrighted works, such as source code and user manuals for internet routers, antenna technology, and robot testing technology," the Department of Justice said.
False statenments about Iran operations
Prosecutors also alleged that Huawei did business in countries subject to US sanctions including Iran and North Korea.
Huawei then made false statements to both US government officials and banks in order to hide this activity, prosecutors said.

"Few crimes are as serious as Huawei's decades-long pattern of endangering US national security, violating the sanctity of US commerce, and impeding the ‌enforcement of ​US laws," US Attorney Joseph Nocella said.

blocks.caption: Lawyer Brian Heberlig represented Huawei in courtImage: Jane Rosenberg/REUTERS

blocks.text: Huawei to appeal verdict
Huawei continued to deny the allegations even after the verdict on Tuesday.
"We believe the government's remaining charges are equally without legal or factual merit," the company said in a statement.

"The five trade secret-related disputes cited by the government were all civil matters that were resolved over the past two decades. No court ever found Huawei liable for willful intellectual property misappropriation, and the company was never ordered to pay damages for trade secret misappropriation."
The company's lawyer, Brian Heberlig, said: "We fully expect to appeal."
Huawei is set to be sentenced next September and could face billions of dollars in penalties.

articles.title: Lies, a disguise and surfboard bags: how a jealous Sydney policeman tried to cover up double murder
articles.summary: Beau Lamarre was on Wednesday found guilty of murdering his ex Jesse Baird, and Baird's new partner Luke Davies.

blocks.text: Lies, a disguise and surfboard bags: how a jealous Sydney policeman tried to cover up double murder

blocks.caption: Image caption, Thousands of hours of CCTV footage helped convict Beau Lamarre

blocks.text: Image source, NSW Supreme Court
Thousands of hours of CCTV footage helped convict Beau Lamarre
ByHelen Livingstone
Sydney
It was just after 09:00 on a warm February morning when CCTV picked up a man dressed as an UberEats rider hovering on a sidewalk in one of Sydney's wealthiest neighbourhoods.

He dawdled for around 20 minutes, "steeling himself for what he was about to do" prosecutors say, before disappearing out of sight. Minutes later another CCTV camera captured the sound of gunshots ringing out.
Former police officer Beau Lamarre, 31, was on Wednesday found guilty of murdering his former partner Jesse Baird, a TV presenter, and Luke Davies, Baird's new partner, with his work-issued gun.

In February 2024, the bloodied belongings of Baird and Davies were found in a skip in the suburb of Cronulla, sparking a frantic search for the couple. It culminated in the discovery of their bodies on a rural property, partially buried beneath sticks and debris.

blocks.caption: Image caption, Luke Davies (left) and Jesse Baird had been dating only months when they were gunned down

blocks.text: Image source, Supplied: Jesse Baird
Luke Davies (left) and Jesse Baird had been dating only months when they were gunned down
During a two-month trial filled with at-times extraordinary testimony and a wealth of CCTV evidence, the court heard Lamarre had planned his crime over months.

Jurors watched CCTV of the then police officer purchasing a surfboard bag in which to put Baird's body, after casually sizing it up against a friend in the shop, and heard from a stream of former friends and colleagues who testified that Lamarre asked them for advice about everything from mobile phone signals to where he could buy a gun.
One recounted the chilling moment Lamarre told her that if he were ever to murder someone, he would leave their belongings in a dumpster and hide the body in bushland where they would never be found.
"What would you do if I told you I killed somebody? Would you help me hide the body?" he asked, according to her testimony.
Later, Lamarre asked for help in covering up the killings; his friends - none of whom have been implicated - say they began receiving panicked calls and odd requests from him.

One told the court Lamarre persuaded her to go for a drive in the country, during which he tried to dispose of the bodies at the family farm of a man he'd met on a dating app. Over the speakers, he played Taylor Swift's No Body, No Crime.
Dark infatuation

Baird, 26, and Lamarre - a one-time celebrity blogger who also had his own swimwear line on the side of his police work - met in a nightclub in October 2022. For Lamarre, it quickly became an infatuation, but for Baird, an AFL referee and former Network Ten presenter, the relationship appeared to be casual.
After discovering in April 2023 that Lamarre had gone through messages on his phone, and unfollowed other men on his Instagram account, Baird broke it off.

But Lamarre's obsession only grew. He watched Baird having sex with another man through his bedroom window, broke into his house multiple times, deleting contacts on his phone and turning on location settings so that he could engineer meetings with the TV presenter.

On one occasion Baird woke up to find Lamarre in his bedroom; not realising who it was, he chased him down the street. Lamarre was also convicted of aggravated break and enter over that incident on Wednesday.
Prosecutor Brett Hatfield said Baird was "oblivious to the accused's scheming and manipulations", and the pair briefly rekindled the relationship before Baird ended it definitively in November.
He'd discovered Lamarre had, again, been accessing his phone and had attempted to ward off a love rival by pretending to have received flowers from Baird.
'The beginning of the plan for murder'

blocks.caption: Image caption, Beau Lamarre pictured at the annual Gay and Lesbian Mardi Gras parade in Sydney in 2020

blocks.text: Image source, EPA-EFE/REX/Shutterstock
Beau Lamarre pictured at the annual Gay and Lesbian Mardi Gras parade in Sydney in 2020
His pride wounded, Hatfield said Lamarre's thoughts turned to a "darker place": "revenge".
He asked an old friend if her ex-partner could get him a gun: "This was the beginning of the plan for the murder," the prosecutor said.

In the months leading up to the killings, Lamarre bought a burner phone, a motorcycle helmet, and practised shooting in the woods. On holiday with a friend in Bali in January 2024 he tried to buy a silencer.
While his murder plans percolated, he also began lashing out with petty acts of malice, prosecutors said, such as putting water in the fuel tank of Baird's car.
But at the same time as he plotted, Lamarre was still trying to win his ex back.
On one occasion he pressured a friend to send Baird a 1,600-word message he had himself composed, claiming that he had cancer, and may need to have his arm amputated.
Under questioning in court, he said a naturopath he couldn't remember the name of had diagnosed him with "a form of sporadic cancer".

By the end of 2023, Baird had met and hit it off with Davies, 29. "It was early days but they were both smitten with each other," his mother, Helen Baird, told the court. He sent her a picture of the pair at a Pink concert. "I just sent a big love heart and said 'I'm so happy for both of you'."

blocks.caption: Image caption, Jesse Baird and Luke Davies at the Pink concert shortly before they were killed

blocks.text: Jesse Baird and Luke Davies at the Pink concert shortly before they were killed

Early on the morning of 19 February, Lamarre picked up a hire car he had asked his mother to rent and drove to Baird's home. After waiting several hours for Baird's housemates to leave, while disguised as an UberEats driver, he let himself in with a key he had copied.

Lamarre told the court he had been at Baird's home to pick up some belongings, including a A$25,000 (US$16,500, £12,600) Cartier ring, and had disguised himself to avoid the embarrassment of being recognised if anyone was home.

He claimed he let himself in when no one answered the door, and the two men were killed in separate struggles. He argued that Baird had been holding a knife and the first shot was fired to disarm him, and the second by accident. Davies shot himself when he grabbed the gun, Lamarre said.
But prosecutors told the jury Baird was shot in the back and then once again through his temple as he lay gravely wounded on the kitchen floor.
The evidence, Hatfield said, pointed to one thing only: "an execution".
Davies was then shot through a bedroom door as he tried to call emergency services. The court heard the panic in his voice as the seconds-long call was replayed before it dropped out.
Covering tracks
After that, Lamarre set about trying to hide the evidence of what Hatfield called his "brazen and shocking murders".
One of his first actions was to call a friend. He testified Lamarre confessed he had "killed people" and asked him to take a day off work "to help him clean up his mess".
Later Lamarre pretended the call was a joke, saying, "Did you like my Oscar performance? Got you".

Meanwhile, Lamarre went to a DIY store to purchase mops, bleach and bin bags. After returning to Baird's house to clean up, he left the bodies wrapped in surfboard bags and tarpaulins in the courtyard.
Baird had been set to move out that week, and Lamarre used Baird's phone to reassure his housemates he had hired an Airtasker to move his belongings, adding, "I might be flying to Perth tonight".
Baird's housemates quickly spotted the surfboard bags when they returned home, snapping a photograph tendered in court which showed "red liquid" seeping out.
"I thought it was rusted water from the outdoor furniture," one of the women said.
The surfboard bags were gone the next morning.

blocks.caption: Image caption, Lamarre was captured on CCTV sizing up a surfboard bag in the days before the murders

blocks.text: Lamarre was captured on CCTV sizing up a surfboard bag in the days before the murders

Lamarre had hired a van, and over the next two days made more trips to the DIY store and a sports shop to buy gumboots, a wheelbarrow, bigger surfboard bags and 10kg weights. He squeezed in a hospital appointment for a minor procedure and paused for a sushi date with a friend, CCTV showing him laughing and eating as the bodies lay in the back of his van.
On 21 February, he picked up another friend in the van for what she thought was lunch.

There were blue tarps in the back and it smelled "lemony", she told the court. She "wasn't allowed to put the windows up or turn the aircon off" as they motored towards Goulburn, 200km southwest of Sydney, stopping only at another DIY store, where he asked her to buy an angle grinder.
His friend told the court she remembers Lamarre playing No Body, No Crime at some point: "It's a very niche song."
Arriving at a farm owned by a Hinge date's family, Lamarre used the angle grinder to cut through a padlock, making his way to a dam where he unsuccessfully tried to sink the bodies.

It was now late at night and he drove his friend, by this time upset and confused, home before returning to retrieve the bodies. He then left them in the van, parked in Sydney overnight, before driving once more to Goulburn, where he dumped the bodies near a monastery.

Later that day he visited another friend, telling her to look up the definition of schizophrenia and asking whether he could use her hose, because "there was a bit of blood he had to scrub off" the hired van, the court heard.
Lamarre faces life in prison

blocks.caption: Image caption, The deaths of Baird and Davies triggered an outpouring of horror in Sydney

blocks.text: Image source, Getty
The deaths of Baird and Davies triggered an outpouring of horror in Sydney
By this time police were closing in, and on 23 February Lamarre went to turn himself in at Bondi police station. On the way, he called a police helpline.

"I've been bullied by multiple New South Wales police force members," he told the woman on the other end of the line. "All this stress and trauma and psychological abuse and trauma - did I say trauma already? - has caused me to not sleep, get anxious, it's caused me to have some symptoms of schizophrenia."
"Actually sorry, you know what, can you just... delete that whole thing. We'll just keep it short and sweet."
He wasn't sure when he'd be back to work, he said. Shortly afterwards he was arrested and charged with murder, and the bodies of Baird and Davies were found four days later.
Lamarre's lawyer John Stratton insisted he'd acted in self-defence and had "panicked" realising how the scene would look to outsiders.
The former police officer did plenty of "foolish" and "unusual" things - "He was, it's fair to say, a poorly behaved boyfriend," Stratton said - but that did not make him a murderer.
Ultimately, however, the jury was not convinced and took just over an hour to convict him. He will be sentenced in March and faces life in prison.

articles.title: Thomas Markle indicted in US for possessing child sex abuse images
articles.summary: The FBI arrested Markle on 6 November after a search of a storage unit he had allegedly rented in Los Angeles uncovered the abuse material.

blocks.text: Thomas Markle, the father of Meghan, Duchess of Sussex has been indicted by a federal grand jury in Los Angeles for possessing child sex abuse images.

Markle, who remains in custody in Florida, allegedly possessed materials that include at least one image involving a prepubescent minor and a minor under 12 years old, court documents filed in California show.
The 82-year-old has denied possessing images of child sex abuse. He is expected to be arraigned in Los Angeles in the coming weeks.
Last week, a judge in Florida declared Prince Harry's father-in-law mentally competent to stand trial.
The FBI arrested Markle on 6 November at an elderly care home in Florida on a single federal charge of possessing child sexual abuse material. He now faces two counts.
US attorney Bill Essayli said Markle faces a maximum of 20 years in prison on each count if convicted.
His arrest came after a search of a storage unit he had allegedly rented in Los Angeles for almost two decades uncovered the abuse material.
Markle was initially released on conditional bail but was then ordered to stay in jail pending trial after allegedly removing a location monitoring device.

In the indictment, filed by the US Attorney's Office in the Central District of California, Markle is accused of knowingly possessing 35mm film negatives on 30 October and 4 November that contained child sexual abuse materials.
The US Attorney's Office said that during both instances Markle allegedly knew the images contained such materials.
Inside the storage units, federal agents found two images that depict an adult man - whom a witness identified as Markle - with an underage child, the US attorney's office said.

They also alleged that a third image appears to depict a child in a room believed to be part of a motel chain in the Philippines. Markle moved to the Philippines last year after he had a series of strokes, and he lived in Cebu until May.
"The affidavit also describes additional photographs that appear to show Markle with children in various stages of undress," prosecutors said.

articles.title: China investigates politburo star in Xi Jinping’s latest purge
articles.summary:
Chen Jining, regarded as a contender for higher office, becomes the fourth member of China’s elite politburo to be investigated since 2025

China has launched an investigation into Shanghai’s…

blocks.text: China has launched an investigation into Shanghai’s Communist party chief Chen Jining, a member of the country’s elite politburo, the state-run Xinhua news agency unexpectedly announced on Tuesday, marking the fourth member of the top leadership ⁠body to be probed since ⁠2025.
China’s anti-graft watchdog is investigating ​Chen for “suspected severe violations of discipline and laws”, Xinhua said, using a common euphemism for corruption.

For Chinese officials, especially those of Chen’s ⁠rank, the public announcement of an investigation by the central commission for discipline inspection generally signals their eventual political downfall.
The investigation marks a further escalation in President Xi Jinping’s widening anti-graft campaign, which has thinned the party’s senior leadership ranks and depleted the military’s top command.
Before the announcement of the Chen probe, three politburo members from the once 24-member body formed in 2022 – He Weidong, Zhang ⁠Youxia and Ma Xingrui – had already been purged.

Chen, 62, had an unusual rise through China’s official ranks. ​An environmental scientist by training, he earned a doctorate from Imperial ‌College London and rose through China’s elite Tsinghua ‌University to become its president.

He entered government as China’s environmental protection minister in 2015 – just as Xi was elevating pollution control and ecological protection as ‌policy priorities – before becoming mayor of Beijing. He joined the politburo in 2022 and was named party boss of Shanghai, China’s financial hub.

blocks.caption: Chen Jining waves the Paralympic flag during the Closing Ceremony for the 2018 Winter Paralympics in South Korea, in his role as mayor of Beijing.  Photograph: Adam Davy/PA

blocks.text: He has long been viewed as a political star and a plausible contender for higher national office. The investigation into him took analysts by surprise.
Joseph Torigian, an expert in Chinese politics at American University, called it a reminder of “how little we really understand about what’s going on in Chinese elite politics”.

At a gathering of leaders last month, the ruling Communist party pledged to keep waging indefinitely its high-pressure anti-corruption campaign, which has ensnared millions within ‌China’s vast bureaucracy and has seen hundreds of top officials purged, including those once thought untouchable.

Xi had called on the party to “turn the blade inward” and unleash a revolution on itself and eradicate “viruses and impurities” that corrode its health. The party views ​the drive as essential to ensuring its long-term survival.
“No matter who they are, how high their position, or how great their contributions, anyone who engages in corruption will surely receive no leniency,” Xi said in January.

Chen’s unexpected probe “sends a signal that there’s no letting up in the anti-corruption drive and the party’s ’self-revolution,’” said China expert Jean Christopher Mittelstaedt of the University of Zurich.
“If anything, it continues to intensify.”

Chen, who last appeared in public last week, was a good candidate to ​watch for elevation to the ‌politburo standing committee in the ​party’s top reshuffle next year, Mittelstaedt said. “This ​sends a signal that nobody is safe.”
The Shanghai party secretary post is one of China’s most prestigious provincial-level positions and has often served as a springboard to top leadership roles.
Xi himself briefly served as Shanghai’s party boss in 2007 before joining the politburo’s standing committee, the country’s highest decision-making body.

Shanghai’s senior party leadership pledged loyalty to Beijing and understanding of the need to “see things through ⁠to the end” ⁠after Chen ​was put under investigation, the financial hub’s official paper said on Wednesday.
