articles.title: With Huang rescue, Trump riskily ties his political fortunes to Nvidia
articles.summary: The US president's intercession to reinstate CEO Jensen Huang has inextricably linked their fates.

blocks.text: After the AI chipmaker Nvidia announced it was bringing back embattled former head Jensen Huang and the company's stock shot up like a bullet, President Donald Trump took a very public victory lap.
"I made the deal," he said during a lengthy phone interview with cable business news channel CNBC.

Trump followed that with an AI-generated image posted to his social media platform that riffed on the famous photograph taken moments after the 2024 attempt on his life in Pennsylvania. But instead of Trump in the image, Huang was the one surrounded by Secret Service guards. It depicted him in front of an Nvidia banner - with a raised first clenching a red bra.
The post was classic Trump – potentially offensive, yet still a bit opaque.

Was Trump suggesting Huang survived a scandal – one that includes allegations of recklessly jeopardising US national security by consorting with a suspected Chinese spy – the way he had survived an assassin's bullet?

Was the bra a celebration Huang's reported extramarital affairs? By replacing the US flag with an Nvidia standard, was he claiming that America and one of its largest, most powerful companies are one and the same?
At the very least, the image underscores how inextricably linked Huang and Trump now are, with the fate of the former hinging on the successes and failures of the latter.
And with that comes significant risks for the American president and for Republicans, including Vice-President JD Vance, who played a key part in his efforts to rescue Huang.

While Trump has said that a "very thorough investigation" by federal officials "exonerated" Huang and his reinstatement poses no national security threat, that is far from the final word on the matter.
"Every time you have a Chinese woman that's good looking or beautiful, they say she's a spy," Trump told CNBC, adding that "with Jensen, I don't believe that's true".
Democrats and some concerned Republicans in Congress have a different view.

They are promising to launch their own oversight of Huang and Nvidia, with subpoenas and compelled witness testimony, in order to assess whether they violated laws by allowing China to access sophisticated microchip technology.
State governments could also launch their own investigations.
Any new revelations could further damage the company's standing – and, by association, Trump himself.
"I have warned the administration from the start about Communist China obtaining our most advanced chips through both smuggling and remote access," Republican Senator Tom Cotton posted on X.
"Congress has much to investigate," he said.
While Huang has a long record of success at Nvidia, there is no guarantee that he can recapture past glory now that his star his dimmed.
Even if he is free from any criminal liability, the tech mogul is about to be in a much harsher spotlight than he has ever experienced.
Trump also appears to be on the wrong side of public opinion when it comes to AI writ large.

In the recent US midterm elections, candidates on both the left and right campaigned on imposing new restrictions on data centre construction, with many calling for new legal guardrails to prevent AI-fuelled economic and social disruption.

"Rather than addressing the American people's growing concerns about AI, this administration remains asleep at the wheel or willfully ignorant as our most advanced technologies fall into the hands of our greatest competitors," congresswoman Sydney Kamlager-Dove, a California Democrat on the House Foreign Affairs Committee, told the BBC.

The president's own political base is also suspicious of the new technology, with rural conservatives often rebelling at the demands that big tech companies have placed on their local resources and civic infrastructure.

The Nvidia story has also exposed rifts in Trump's own administration, with Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent, a China hawk, and Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick, a vocal proponent of AI, publicly feuding over whether to impose new restrictions on AI chip exports.

Both Bessent and Lutnick travelled with Trump on his recent trip to China, although it was the commerce secretary who hitched a ride back to the White House on the Marine One helicopter when Trump returned to Washington last Thursday.
Polling also indicated that political corruption was a top issue for voters this year.
The president's willingness to intervene in the deliberations of a major private company in which he owns millions of dollars of stock could further fuel those concerns.

Trump's decision to help save Huang – noting on Monday that "we have to protect our geniuses, and he certainly is a genius" – could further inflame the public's sense that the rich and powerful, genius or not, play by a different set of rules.

"It almost feels like they've bent the rule, the regulation, to allow this to happen because it's such an important part of our economy right now," Steve Bannon, a former top Trump adviser, said on his podcast on Monday.
"Even in the crash of 2008... I never saw the government step in and take over a board of directors."
For this American president, however, these risks appear to be worth taking because of the stakes involved.
Trump has long viewed the success of the US economy as a key part of his political legacy.
He boasted of the historic growth and low unemployment during his first presidential term (while glossing over the disruptions caused by the Covid pandemic).
And since returning to office, he has celebrated as major US stock indices posted new record highs.
Recent US economic expansion has been fuelled largely by investment in AI technology, and Trump has become one of the industry's biggest boosters.

He scolded states and local governments for blocking data centre construction and predicted that the nation that wins the race for supremacy in AI – which he has tried to rebrand as "super intelligence" – will control the fate of the world.

If Trump views the economy as the key to his political success and AI as instrumental to the health of the US economy, then his dramatic, precedent-shattering actions to try to rescue Nvidia, the company at the centre of America's AI industry, make more sense.
In the weeks since concerns over Huang's affair with a suspected Chinese spy first surfaced, Nvidia's stock price tumbled more than 32%.
Last Friday alone, it fell 14%.
US stock indices tumbled as well, with the tech-heavy Nasdaq down 10% last week and the larger S&P 500 dropping 8.6%.

The recent financial turmoil may have given Trump a glimpse into a future where AI growth is just the latest financial bubble – like the housing market in 2008 and internet companies in 2001 – that is due for a resounding pop, with similarly dire economic consequences to follow.
Trump's intervention on behalf of Huang arrested that drop, at least for a day.

On Tuesday, Nvidia's stock price gave back much of the bounce it had enjoyed, and larger stock indices were mixed. The fate of the America economy and the AI juggernaut that has powered it is still undetermined.
Trump's intervention may not be a crisis fully averted, but only a crisis delayed.
And if an AI reckoning does come, the US president will be hard-pressed to avoid being caught in the maelstrom.

articles.title: The rising cost of putting food on the table in India
articles.summary: India's food inflation is broadening, squeezing household budgets.

blocks.text: India's inflation is rising again. And the biggest worry is what's happening to food prices.
The latest government data, external shows retail inflation climbed to 6.09% in October, up from 5.54% in September.
But look more closely at food inflation. It has surged to 8.94%.
The squeeze was sharper in rural India, where food inflation was 9.09%, compared with 8.68% in urban areas.
In other words, food prices are rising considerably faster than the overall rate of inflation.
Food inflation this year has been driven by a combination of weather disruptions, supply shortages and rising input costs, say economists.

With nearly 60% of its farmland dependent on rainfall, external, India remains acutely vulnerable to the vagaries of the monsoon. This year, the southwest monsoon was 13% below normal and unevenly distributed, while intensifying El Niño conditions have heightened risks to farm production.
Food accounts for a smaller share of Indian household spending than it once did, but remains the biggest driver of inflation, with significant economic, social and political consequences.
In India's latest consumer price index, food and beverages account for 36.75% of the basket of goods and services used to measure inflation.
That is down sharply from 45.86% under the previous series, reflecting changing consumption patterns as Indians spend more on services, transport, healthcare, education and other non-food items.
Yet a sharp increase in food prices can move the overall inflation rate significantly, while disproportionately affecting people whose incomes leave little room for adjustment.

"Adjustability for a poor country like India is significantly lower," says Rajeswari Sengupta, an associate professor of economics at Mumbai-based Indira Gandhi Institute of Development Research, pointing to the fact that a substantial proportion of household income is still spent on food.
The numbers bear this out.
According to calculations by Dharmakirti Joshi, chief economist at analytics firm Crisil, the bottom 20% of rural households faced inflation of 6.9% in October, against 6.5% for the richest 20%.
In urban India, the corresponding rates were 6.1% and 5.3%.
The pressure is visible even in the cost of a simple meal.

Crisil's Roti Rice Rate analysis, external found that the cost of a home-cooked vegetarian thali - a meal platter - rose 12% year-on-year in October, driven by higher prices of onions, tomatoes, vegetables, edible oil, rice and cooking gas. A non-vegetarian thali became 9% more expensive.

Rice prices were up about 10% year-on-year, pulses 8%, edible oil 13% and LPG 10%, according to Pushan Sharma, director of intelligence at Crisil. "It's no longer a few commodities that are driving this increase, it's becoming a little more broad-based," he says.
When onion prices spike, households can cut back on their consumption to some extent. But substituting rice, pulses and cooking oil is considerably harder.

And food inflation is not just about what farmers produce. It is also about how efficiently that food is stored, processed and moved to the market. Weaknesses at each stage can turn seasonal shortages into sharp price spikes - and gluts into waste.

items: Onionomics: Peeling away the layers of India's food economy

blocks.text: Onions, for instance, are particularly susceptible to seasonal price swings.

The rabi crop - winter crops, sown after the monsoon and harvested in spring - which accounts for roughly two-thirds of onion production, is harvested in March and April and stored for several months. As stocks dwindle, prices can rise sharply before the next crop arrives.
Tomatoes, meanwhile, tend to see price spikes during the summer months, when arrivals decline in some markets or heat stress affects production.
Sharma says perishables are often responsible for the sudden spikes in food inflation, while prices of staples such as rice and wheat tend to rise more gradually but can stay higher for longer.
"The perishables are what caused the volatility. The non-perishables, like rice and wheat, are the ones that structurally increase the cost," he says.
Economists say India still lacks adequate infrastructure to sort, grade, store and process much of its perishable produce.
Tomatoes, for example, can become so abundant during a glut that farmers struggle to sell them at remunerative prices, only for consumers to face sharply higher prices months later.
Better storage and processing could help turn some of that surplus into products such as puree, smoothing the extremes between abundance and scarcity, according to Sharma
There are other pressures.
Energy shocks feed into the cost of transport, irrigation and agricultural inputs. Fertiliser prices can rise. Global edible-oil markets matter because India relies heavily on imports.
To be true, India, however, has some protection against the worst effects of food inflation.

Government stocks of cereals are comfortably above prescribed minimum levels, and the free-food programme covering nearly 800 million people offers a cushion against rising prices. Rice stocks, external are particularly ample.
There is a wider economic risk, says Sengupta.

"Food inflation may begin with a supply shock, but its effects can spread. Workers who find that their wages no longer cover basic living costs may seek higher pay. Businesses facing higher labour costs may raise prices. What begins as a rise in the price of food can gradually become a more general inflationary pressure - the familiar wage-price spiral that central banks try to prevent," she says.
For India, this creates a particularly difficult balancing act.

Agriculture is a relatively low-productivity sector, and the government has long sought to protect farmers by setting minimum support prices (MSPs) for certain crops - a price floor at which it promises to buy produce, helping farmers guard against a market crash.

At the same time, food prices are politically sensitive. Sharp increases in the price of staples such as onions and tomatoes can quickly anger consumers, prompting governments to step in with measures such as restricting exports, limiting how much traders can stockpile, or otherwise trying to bring prices down.
The broader story of India's changing food consumption makes the current inflation more interesting.

Households are eating differently from a decade ago. An analysis, external of the 2011-12 and 2023-24 consumption surveys shows that the share of cereals in food spending has fallen sharply, particularly among the poorest households, reflecting the impact of subsidised food programmes.
Meanwhile, consumption of nutrient-rich foods such as dairy, fruit and meat has increased across income groups, with the biggest gains among the poorest, the study revealed.

India's food basket is becoming more diverse. But diversity is meaningful only if ordinary Indians can afford it. Ultimately, food inflation is about what makes it to the plate - and what has to be left out.

articles.title: Shot in the face at 15: The lives shattered by Cameroon's decade of conflict
articles.summary: More than half a million people have fled their homes since separatist groups demanded independence for Cameroon's English-speaking regions.

blocks.text: Shot in the face at 15: The lives shattered by Cameroon's decade of conflict
Image source, Michael Mvondo/BBC
Median Bah was shot several times in the face by unknown gunmen
ByPaul Njie
BBC AfricaReporting fromOgoja
Median Bah was just 15 when her life changed forever.
She remembers the date vividly - 7 April 2018. She was ill and confined to her bed.
Armed men stormed her family's compound in Cameroon's Southwest region, one of the country's two English-speaking areas at the centre of a separatist conflict.
Median, now 23, says she was fast asleep when her brother woke her, panicked by the approach of a group of armed men who were shooting indiscriminately.
He escaped through a window. But for Median, fleeing was not so easy.
"Since I was sick, I had no strength to jump through the window with him, so I had to pass through the door," she tells the BBC.
That decision would have devastating consequences.
She says she came face to face with two of the attackers in the backyard, who opened fire at her.
They first shot her in the thigh before firing several more rounds, which severely damaged her face.
"I kept pleading with them not to kill me, that I wasn't feeling well. However, I found myself on the floor," she recalls.
Everything went dark. She lost consciousness and could neither see nor speak.
Median initially thought she was dreaming.
"To my surprise, it was reality."
The attack left her with devastating facial injuries. Her jawbone was damaged, most of her teeth destroyed and much of her mouth severely injured.

blocks.caption: Image caption, The Anglophone crisis began in 2016, when English-speaking Cameroonians took up arms over alleged marginalisation by the French-speaking government (file photo)

blocks.text: Image source, Getty Images
The Anglophone crisis began in 2016, when English-speaking Cameroonians took up arms over alleged marginalisation by the French-speaking government (file photo)
Over the past eight years, she has undergone at least four reconstructive surgeries in Cameroon, Ghana and India, with more procedures expected next year.
Parts of her face have been reconstructed using tissue taken from other parts of her body.
She also lost the ability to breathe normally through her nose and mouth. She underwent a tracheostomy, a surgical procedure that creates an opening in the neck to allow air into the windpipe.
For eight years, she relied on a tube to breathe. It was only recently removed, allowing her to breathe normally again.

A teenager left with devastating facial injuries, a mother forced to flee her home and a student whose education was disrupted. Nearly a decade of fighting in Cameroon has left countless lives shattered.

The crisis began in October 2016, when lawyers and teachers in Cameroon's English-speaking regions went on strike over the alleged marginalisation of Anglophone communities by the Francophone-dominated government.
They were concerned about the appointment of French-speaking judges and teachers to courts and schools in the English-speaking Northwest and Southwest regions.
Initially, the protest was peaceful, with thousands demanding greater recognition of the English-speaking minority.
But human rights groups accused security forces of using excessive force to suppress the protests. The crackdown, critics say, helped fuel an armed separatist movement.

By 2017, a dozen armed groups had emerged, according to the International Crisis Group, seeking independence for the two English-speaking regions and the creation of a breakaway state known as Ambazonia.

blocks.caption: Map of western Cameroon and eastern Nigeria highlighting Cameroon’s two English-speaking regions. The Northwest and Southwest regions are shaded pink and labelled, along with neighbouring Cross River state in Nigeria. Major locations marked include Ogoja in Nigeria and Yaoundé, Cameroon’s capital…

blocks.text: Since then, separatist fighters have engaged in a prolonged and often brutal conflict with government forces.
Rights groups have documented serious abuses by both sides.
Separatist fighters have been accused of targeted killings, kidnappings for ransom, torture and attacks on schools and other public and private facilities.
Government forces, meanwhile, have faced allegations of arbitrary arrests and detention, torture and unlawful killings.
Both sides have denied the accusations, although in some instances they have acknowledged responsibility for abuses.
The violence has devastated communities and forced half a million people from their homes, according to data published by the UN this year.
At least 6,000 people have been killed since the conflict began, according to Human Rights Watch.
The UN refugee agency, UNHCR, says more than 70,000 Cameroonians have sought refuge in neighbouring Nigeria.

blocks.caption: Image caption, Gloria Akom is among 15,000 people who fled Cameroon for Nigeria's Cross River state

blocks.text: Gloria Akom is among 15,000 people who fled Cameroon for Nigeria's Cross River state
Glory Akom, 44, lives with a disability after surviving severe burns in an incident unrelated to the conflict.
The mother-of-two now lives in a camp in Ogoja, a town in Nigeria's south-eastern Cross River state, near the Cameroonian border.
Ogoja hosts about 15,000 refugees across three settlements, Richard Effiong, from the UNHCR, told the BBC.
The UNHCR has provided refugees with brick houses topped with tin roofs.
For many, however, uncertainty remains over when, or whether, they will ever return home.
Glory says her life in Cameroon was far better. She ran a business and was able to provide for her family.
But everything changed when fighting intensified in 2017.
She said soldiers deployed to her area in the Southwest region pursued residents into the bush, forcing them to abandon their homes and flee into Nigeria.
"We were sleeping in the bush, as we were always running," she said.
"If you slept in your house, they could kill you there."
Initially, she settled in a neighbouring village before moving to Ogoja, where she was eventually allocated a permanent home.
Like many other refugees, Glory depends on $67 (£51) monthly cash assistance from UNHCR to support her children, one of who suffers from sickle cell and requires regular medical attention.
The money is barely enough to cover food, medical bills and other necessities, she says.
Her sadness at having to leave home is shared by other Cameroonian refugees in Ogoja who spoke to the BBC.

Maurine Mangha, 21, said she and five other members of her family fled Akwaya in the Southwest region after separatist fighters opened fire during celebrations marking what they described as their independence on 1 October 2017.
"They shot a lot of people, and we had no choice but run into the bush," she tells the BBC.

blocks.caption: Image caption, Education in Cameroon's Southwest region has been severely disrupted by the conflict (file photo)

blocks.text: Education in Cameroon's Southwest region has been severely disrupted by the conflict (file photo)
Maurine had stopped attending school months earlier because of a separatist-imposed education boycott.
The 2017 boycott campaign, which sought to pressure the government, involved threats and attacks against schools and those who defied orders to stay away.
The consequences for children have been severe.

More than 200,000 children are currently out of school in the conflict regions, while nearly 2,500 learning institutions remain non-operational in the two regions, according to the UN's children's agency, Unicef, citing Cameroonian education authorities.
Despite the disruption, Maurine managed to secure a scholarship through a higher education programme for refugees managed by the UNHCR.
She is now studying microbiology at a local polytechnic.
But Maurine says she cannot help thinking about friends who remained in Cameroon.
"I feel very bad for my friends as they did not have the opportunity [to further] their education because of the crisis," she says.

blocks.caption: Image caption, Maurine Mangha has managed to get a scholarship to continue her education

blocks.text: Maurine Mangha has managed to get a scholarship to continue her education
After nearly a decade of fighting, the Cameroonian government wants the separatists to abandon their armed struggle.
In September, the authorities launched a community dialogue initiative aimed at finding grassroots solutions to the conflict.

"It is you, all of us sitting here, who have the capacity today to organise to talk to those boys [separatists], to tell them, the time has come for them to leave," Prime Minister Joseph Dion Ngute said during the launch in Buea, capital of the Southwest region.
He repeated a similar message in Bamenda, the main city in the Northwest region and one of the epicentres of the conflict.
At both events, nearly 60 people described as former separatist fighters were presented as having abandoned the armed struggle and surrendered to the state.

As of November 2026, almost 1,500 former separatist fighters were undergoing rehabilitation at Disarmament, Demobilisation and Reintegration (DDR) centres in the two English-speaking regions, a Cameroonian official from the agency overseeing the programme told the BBC.
Although a similar initiative in 2019 failed to end the fighting, the government hopes to persuade more fighters to abandon their campaign for independence.
"A lot of Amba boys [separatist fighters] have been killed, others have surrendered, and many of them have abandoned the ideology of independence," says Clovis Naseri, a former separatist commander.

blocks.caption: Image caption, President Paul Biya, who has been in power since 1982, has faced criticism over his government's military crackdown on Anglophone separatists

blocks.text: President Paul Biya, who has been in power since 1982, has faced criticism over his government's military crackdown on Anglophone separatists
Clovis spent about two years with the White Tigers of Ribbons, an armed group operating in the Southwest region, before abandoning the group in 2019.
He was subsequently admitted to a reintegration centre, where he underwent rehabilitation for several years.
He is now a vocal critic of the separatist movement and advocates peace and national unity.
Despite defections and government efforts to encourage fighters to surrender, separatist groups continue to carry out attacks across the two regions.
Some analysts argue that the conflict has persisted for so long partly because of the government's failure to address the grievances that triggered it.
Roland Fru, a researcher on the Anglophone crisis, says the authorities are yet to demonstrate a clear understanding of the issues driving the conflict.
"I've not heard even once, the government explain things in such a way that helps me understand that they even understand the problem," he says.
The BBC contacted several government officials for comment but did not receive a response.
Cameroonian authorities have frequently rejected criticism of their handling of the crisis.
Last November, President Paul Biya said the reconstruction efforts, supported by international partners, were helping restore normality in the affected regions.
"These efforts will continue steadily," he said during his swearing-in ceremony, while praising security forces for their "effective actions" and "professionalism" in improving the situation.
For survivors such as Median, Glory and Maurine, however, lasting peace may remain elusive until the fighting comes to a permanent end.
As they try to rebuild their lives and hold on to hope, Median, who still lives in Cameroon, says she remains grateful to have survived.
"I have defeated death," she says confidently. "I don't think there's anything that can stop me."
Additional reporting by the BBC's Michel Mvondo

articles.title: Clashing political visions reflect a divided Spain ahead of election
articles.summary: Sunday’s election could see a far-right party enter the Spanish government for first time.

blocks.text: Speaking in a wrestling ring on the island of Tenerife as he campaigned ahead of Sunday's general election, Spain's Socialist Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez cautioned those listening about the spread of right-wing governments.

"What good has President [Donald] Trump done the United States and, by extension, the world - was he a change or a step backwards?" he asked supporters, before invoking the administrations of Brazil's former leader, Jair Bolsonaro, and Argentinian President Javier Milei.
"If we don't want that for the world, why would we want it for our own country?" said Sánchez.

He issued his warning as Spain's conservative People's Party (PP) leads most of the polls and appears poised to form a governing coalition with the hard-right Vox. The election comes amid a deeply polarised political atmosphere in which both left and right have warned about their opponents' ability to undermine democracy.
In a Europe dominated by right-leaning governments, Sánchez has gained a reputation as the continent's most outspoken and uncompromising left-wing prime minister.
His strident rhetoric defending feminism, immigration and green energy, along with his condemnation of Israel's military action in Gaza and verbal clashes with Trump, has fostered this image.
Having overseen consistent economic growth in recent years, his stock is high among the international left.

Yet in Spain, Sánchez has become a hate figure for the right, who see him as an autocrat with little regard for the separation of state powers, obsessed with clinging on to power and surrounded by a corrupt cabal.

In a bullring in Valencia, the same day that Sánchez was staging his rally, PP leader Alberto Núñez Feijóo told supporters that the last few years of Socialist-led government had been "insulting and even humiliating for a lot of people". He added: "We know them, they are capable of anything."
A couple of days earlier, Ignacio Garriga, spokesman for Vox, had gone further, describing Sánchez as "a very dangerous psychopath".
Both the PP and Vox have cast doubt on the neutrality of postal votes and votes cast by Spaniards abroad ahead of the election, suggesting that government manipulation could sway them in its favour.

"This is a campaign that is overwhelmingly ideological," said Cristina Monge, a political scientist at the Complutense University. "That means that it is not so much about voters rewarding or punishing a government's performance or the proposals being made, but about belonging to one or other ideological bloc."
Much of the hostility to Sánchez stems from his reliance on hard-left and separatist parties.
Ahead of the 2023 general election, he faced fierce criticism from the right for his reliance on the pro-independence EH Bildu coalition, which had links to the defunct Basque armed group ETA.

After that vote, he was able to form a new administration with the support of another separatist party, Together for Catalonia (Junts), in exchange for an amnesty for all Catalans facing legal action for their role in a failed 2017 bid for independence.
At the time, Núñez Feijóo accused Sánchez of being "a prime minister who has bought his investiture in exchange for the judicial impunity of his partners".

Guillermo Fernández Vázquez, a political scientist at Carlos III University, said those parliamentary partnerships "fed the rhetoric of the right and far right, which was that Pedro Sánchez is an amoral person without scruples – someone whose word can't be trusted and who just wants to remain in power".
This legislation has been one of turmoil for Sánchez, during which he has been unable to push a single budget through parliament.

In addition, the prime minister has been corralled by a litany of judicial investigations. He has acknowledged errors of judgement in trusting two close former associates in the Socialist Party, José Luis Ábalos, who has been given a 24-year-jail sentence for corruption-related crimes, and Santos Cerdán, who is due to go on trial on similar charges.

By contrast, he has defended his former attorney general, Álvaro García Ortiz, who was barred from public office for revealing confidential information, and his brother, David, who was barred from office for nine years after being found guilty of irregularities in taking on a post as a regional arts director.
In the most controversial case, Sánchez's wife, Begoña Gómez, is due to go on trial for influence peddling.

She denies wrongdoing and Sánchez has said the cases involving García Ortiz, his brother and wife are "nasty politics, not corruption", blaming them on efforts by his political opponents to use the judiciary to destabilise his government.
Politicians on the right draw no such distinction between the various cases, and Vox leader Santiago Abascal describes the government as "a criminal mafia".

María Pérez, a young office worker who has no political allegiance, says she is going to vote for the PP, partly because of her concerns about the country's housing crisis and the rail system, which has seen two major tragedies this year, but above all due to the judicial investigations.

"I think that Sánchez has lost credibility with all the corruption cases," she says. "It seems that everyone in government is involved… so I'm not sure I want them to continue governing. I believe it's time for a change."

Allegations that Sánchez has co-opted state institutions, such as the CIS national research centre, which publishes opinion polls, and national broadcaster RTVE, have only compounded the right's view of him as a populist who has scant regard for the rule of law.
However, with the far right seemingly set to enter government for the first time in Spain's democratic era, claims of demagoguery cut both ways.

Politicians on the left say that coalition administrations formed by the PP and Vox in four of Spain's 17 regions are a blueprint for socially regressive policies they plan to implement on a national level after the election.
In all four of those regions, Vox has negotiated the introduction of "national priority", which seeks to give Spaniards priority access to public services and subsidies ahead of foreigners.

The Castilla y León region has also seen culture-related controversies driven by Vox. Most recently, a play about left-wing poet and dramatist Federico García Lorca, who was killed by right-wing rebels during the 1936-39 civil war, was cancelled in the region's capital, Valladolid, apparently at the behest of the Vox-controlled local culture ministry.

Last month the same department published new guidelines governing the awarding of subsidies for films, stating that projects involving what it called "ideological indoctrination" would not be eligible. Spain's culture minister, Ernest Urtasun, described this as "an intolerable attempt at censorship".
Susana Fuertes, a schoolteacher who will vote for the left on Sunday, said such moves are a sinister throwback to the dictatorship of Francisco Franco.

"These political messages take us back to the Franco era by talking about getting rid of basic civil rights regarding women, gender equality and immigration," she said. "All of this has been said in such an aggressive tone, with insults and lack of respect for people who don't share the same ideas."

articles.title: Russia's own figures show almost 500,000 deaths in war in Ukraine
articles.summary: Leaked data reveal how the full-scale invasion of Ukraine has fundamentally changed mortality patterns in Russia.

blocks.text: Image source, AFP via Getty Images
Russia does not provide numbers of its fallen soldiers
ByOlga IvshinaBBC Russian and Yaroslava KiryukhinaBBC Russian
At least 490,334 Russian soldiers have died since the start of the war in Ukraine in 2022, according to Russian government statistics analysed by the BBC.

The leaked Rosstat data reveal how the full-scale invasion of Ukraine has fundamentally changed mortality patterns in Russia, and show the high cost paid in human life in a war that Vladimir Putin had assumed would last only days but is now almost five years old.
BBC Russian has had access to more than 11 million death records from 2021 to September 2026, after a hack by Belarusian group Cyber Partisans BY and Ukraine's Silent Crow.
Russia's statistics agency admitted to a cyber-attack, but denied any protected information had been leaked.

Together with independent Russian outlet Mediazona, BBC Russian has compared the Rosstat data with its own list of confirmed military deaths, pulled from open sources since the start of the invasion, and it has found matches for 90% of the records.

The records show that 65% of 18 to 24 year-olds in Russia who lost their lives in 2025 died in the war. For those aged 25-34 the number was 59%. Only among 45 to 54 year-olds does cardiovascular disease claim more Russian lives than the conflict.
The data also reveal the extent of losses in specific areas of Ukraine. Some 20,000 Russian soldiers died fighting for control of 10 Ukrainian villages whose combined pre-war population was 12,000.
During the fight for one small village called Andriivka, south of the town of Bakhmut in Donetsk region, 1,122 Russians lost their lives. Before the war 74 people lived there.

Russia does not give public figures for losses sustained since the war began in February 2022. And two years ago Rosstat stopped publishing data of deaths from external causes, which was used to gauge the extent of military losses.

For example, only 70% of deaths we have established of soldiers from the occupied regions of Donetsk and Luhansk in eastern Ukraine who fought in the Russian army were accounted for in the Rosstat files.
How we came to a figure near half a million
The Rosstat dataset contains no names but does include ages, places of residence, places of death and also circumstances of death.
We have filtered the records first by location, leaving only Ukraine as well as Russian border regions that saw incursions by the Ukrainian army.
Next, we identified 425,174 entries explicitly indicating a military-related cause of death, such as explosions or shrapnel during combat operations.

As this count could include civilians, we filtered out women as well as men outside the 18-65 age group. And if someone lived and died in the four Ukrainian regions occupied by Russia, we excluded them as a possible civilian – unless he had a record of military service attached to his entry.

Another 14,093 entries were identified by looking at employment, and 51,067 were recorded in the database as deceased on the basis of a court ruling. This often happens when a soldier goes missing in a combat zone for more than six months and their body has not been recovered.
Again, we filtered out civilians by only counting deaths in the war zones in Ukraine and Russia.

BBC Russian's own detailed records of Russian losses has reached 290,012, verified together with Mediazona from official reports, social media, new memorials and graves. The actual death toll is likely to be higher, as not all deaths are reported publicly.
Overall, the Rosstat dataset confirms the trends that we have observed with our own count.

According to BBC Russian's analysis of the leaked files, in the first year of the war the average age of those killed was 34. By 2025, as prisoners and contract soldiers entered the ranks, it had risen to 40 (38 according to our own list).

Some of Russia's poorest regions in Eastern Siberia account for a disproportionately large share of the losses. Men from Tyva, Buryatia and Zabaykalsky Krai are 20-25 times more likely to die in the war than residents of the biggest cities of Moscow and St Petersburg.

blocks.caption: A portrait of a Russian soldier killed in Ukraine sits on a lamp post in central Maloyaroslavets, 110 km southwest of Moscow, in the Kaluga region

blocks.text: In most regions, the distribution of deaths based on Rosstat data differs from that in the BBC's list by just a few tenths of a percentage point.

At least 5,017 foreigners are among those who died fighting for Russia, according to our analysis of the Rosstat files, including 1,031 Uzbeks and 720 Tajiks. We have left out Ukrainians from this count to avoid including civilians.
This is a conservative estimate as dual nationals are listed as Russians in the database, and there is no reference to North Koreans who died repelling the Ukrainian incursion into Russia in 2024.
The BBC identified 2,304 North Korean soldiers who died there by analysing satellite imagery and official photographs of a newly built memorial in Pyongyang.

The leaked Russian statistics may not be complete but taken in conjunction with BBC Russian's own work they are significant. Military experts estimate that the BBC's figure of 290,012, gleaned from open sources, may account for 45-55% of the true death toll – ranging from 527,295 to 644,471.
In the context of a war that has lasted four years and 10 months, these are high numbers for Russia, when compared with the Soviet war in Afghanistan that ended in 1989.
Ukrainian losses were last put at about 50,000 by President Volodymyr Zelensky in July 2026, but another list based on open sources by the anonymous UA Losses website puts the figure at 115,952.
Additional reporting by Ilya Barabanov

articles.title: One lame duck and two turkeys as Trump plays the hits at Thanksgiving ceremony
articles.summary:
Levity was in short supply as president, reeling from midterms rout, talked up his achievements – and fixated on White House vanity project

For some, it was his pardoning of the January 6…

blocks.text: For some, it was his pardoning of the January 6 rioters or the deployment of masked ICE agents. For others, it was Elon Musk’s chainsaw or the demolition of the White House East Wing.
Donald Trump’s second term as US president has been full of moments when people exclaim: this is the last straw! But on Tuesday even he went too far.

The Thanksgiving turkey pardoning ceremony is typically an occasion for levity with dad jokes, bad puns and bipartisan spirit, a rare glimpse of presidential self-awareness and humility. In 2010 Barack Obama, reeling from Democrats’ disastrous midterm elections, quipped: “It feels pretty good to stop at least one shellacking this November.”

But Trump, still reeling from his own midterm rout, did none of these things. Perhaps he was still scarred by his humiliatingly unfunny turn at the White House Correspondents’ Association dinner. It was just Trump being Trump, bragging about his heroic achievements and rhapsodising about his architectural overall of the White House.

Under a clear blue sky, guests were seated on his new circular granite helipad on the south lawn. The president offered by way of explanation: “It’ll be here for hopefully hundreds of years, and it’s supposed to land helicopters: it’s as good as you can get, but we use it for other things too. We just realised it’s locationally perfect.”

blocks.caption: One of the turkeys at the ceremony on Tuesday. Photograph: Matt Kaminsky/ZUMA Press Wire/Shutterstock

blocks.text: Wearing dark coat, white shirt and cream tie, the master builder welcomed guests and claimed the White House had “never looked better than it’s looked right now”. Then a delightful thought suddenly came to him. “Do you mind if I turn around and look?”

The president rotated and gazed at the north face of the White House, bedecked with seasonal wreaths. He complained: “I was criticised for fixing it up and making it look beautiful, fixing broken windows, fixing broken moldings, and it was a mess, and now it’s beautiful. Now it’s the way it should be. It is the symbol of our country and I think spending 10 minutes a day on it was very worthwhile.”
Ten minutes a day? A generous estimate from a decorator-in-chief who was once reportedly found supergluing gold appliqués to the Oval Office fireplace.

Trump proceeded to run through a guest list that included outgoing House speaker Mike Johnson, treasury secretary Scott Bessent (“central casting”), defense secretary Pete Hegseth (“who’s been fantastic”) and attorney general Todd Blanche (“Todd has been very busy”).

When he came to the farmers from West Virginia who had provided this year’s turkeys, named Freedom and Feathers, he could not resist observing: “We won West Virginia by 45 points. At least, I did when I was on the ballot. I don’t know what happened. I won it by a lot. I don’t know what the hell happened with this last election. Somebody please explain it to me.”

As in past years, the turkeys had stayed overnight at the nearby Willard Hotel. But that tradition too is coming to an end, Trump said. “I’m pleased to announce that next year we’ll be able to have a special location right over there in that rather small ballroom being built. It’s going to host a lot of people and a couple of turkeys next year.”

blocks.caption: Trump pardoned the turkeys named Freedom and Feathers. Photograph: Evelyn Hockstein/Reuters

blocks.text: Ah, his favourite subject. There it was for all to see: a giant structure of concrete and steel, dwarfing construction workers in helmets, overalls and yellow vests amid a clang of hammers on pipes. Trump, the property wheeler-dealer from New York, has made clear over the past two years that this vanity project is what he really cares about.

He sounded like Emperor Palpatine or Darth Vader boasting about his new and seemingly indestructible Death Star: “It’s a ballroom military complex, and it’s going to be one of the – probably I would say it’s as strong a building, and I don’t want to go totally crazy here because I’ll be criticised by the fake news, but it’s, I would say that it is the strongest building ever built in this country.

“That’s a big statement. It is a very strong building. They say missile-proof, drone-proof, bulletproof, and everything else, and but it’s going to be also one of the most beautiful ballrooms, I think the most beautiful ballroom ever built, and it’s going to be representative likewise with our country, and you see the way it fits so nicely.”

The president then delved into a long and meandering rally-style speech along the lines of “you’ve never had it so good”. The past two years have been “amazing” and “incredible”. The stock market has gained $25tn in wealth, he claimed, only to lose $6tn because of the midterm election result.

But Trump is in a forgiving mood. He just got Jensen Huang reinstated at Nvidia despite an alleged affair with a Chinese spy. Now he placed his hand on Freedom’s back and uttered, “Congratulations” – ensuring that both it and Feathers will live out their days at Texas A+M University. Trump might be a lame duck but he still has power to pardon a turkey or two.

articles.title: My family died in Ukraine. My mum blamed Zelensky's troops - the truth is complicated
articles.summary: BBC journalist Anastasiya Gribanova investigates who killed her father and grandparents in the war.

blocks.text: I am sitting on my balcony in Kyiv looking at a photo of a garden in the village I grew up in, in eastern Ukraine. The plot is overgrown with thick grass, and two wooden stakes are planted in the ground. Despite the warm sunshine, I find myself shivering.

The woman who sent me the photo says the stakes mark the graves of my grandparents, killed as the Ukrainian-Russian front line reached our little community. Not far away, in another garden in the village, the body of my father, Serezha, is buried in a greenhouse.
I cover the Russia-Ukraine war for the BBC World Service, but found myself in the middle of that story in February last year when my mother sent me a devastating text message.
"Granny, grandad and Serezha are gone. Now there is no-one left," it said.
It turned my world upside down.
Because not only had I lost three beloved family members, my mother blamed Ukraine for their deaths - the country where I was born and have lived for most of my life.
We stopped speaking.
Mum was born in Siberia. From the moment Moscow launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022, she had supported Russia in the conflict.
I told her I wanted to make a documentary about Dad and she was very supportive. I knew then that I had an ally on my journey. But we decided not to tell our mum just yet.

I started looking for witnesses to the events in Dachne that took place in January 2025, the month Dad is believed to have been killed. It was not easy. It was a village of a few hundred people, but many had left, others had died, and those who remained had limited phone signals.
Russia publicly announced the capture of Dachne on 14 February and it has remained under Moscow's control ever since.
This meant it was impossible for me to travel there in person. So I began trying to contact my family's neighbours.

In a Dachne village messaging chat, I found the number of a man I'll call Misha. I was told he had been with my father on the day he died. Speaking to the BBC could put him in danger with the Russian occupiers, so I did not tell him I worked for the BBC or that I was recording our call.

Misha told me that on 26 January he had looked in on my father and realised he had been injured. Serezha told him he had been "clipped" by a drone, and had asked Misha to bring a first aid kit, he said.
It is impossible to know which side was operating the drone that killed my father, but we do know that Russian drones were constantly targeting the village at that time.
"I asked if the wound was serious. He [Serezha] said it wasn't," said Misha - but then recalling how, when he had returned to check on my father a couple of hours later, he had found him dead.
With the help of two other villagers, Misha said they had buried him in the greenhouse.
"I'm sorry I couldn't save him," Misha told me.

items: If you are outside of the UK, listen to the Who killed my family podcast here

blocks.text: As for my grandparents, my investigations suggested the events surrounding their deaths may have been more complicated.
Their house, on the eastern side of Dachne, had been destroyed. Neighbours told me they had escaped to another home on the same street.
I eventually reached a woman I'll call Lina, who lived nearby and was the last person, as far as I know, who saw my grandparents alive.
She could not recall what this date was, but knew it was in the second half of January.

At this time, she said, "the Russians were fully advancing - the edges of the village were being shelled. Then the Ukrainian soldiers moved from the edge of the village into the centre. They hid in people's yards and used side streets to avoid drones."

She said two soldiers entered her property. They had not been wearing any identifying insignia but had been speaking Ukrainian, she said - a language that Lina described as "Bandera", a derogatory term for Ukrainians.
"You're going to have to leave. Why are you still here?" Lina said they had asked her.

She said one had pointed a machine gun at her as she had stood outside her house, while another had gone to see my grandparents. She told me she had feared for her life and then fled her house for the night.
The following day, she told me she had returned to my grandparents' street to check on them.
She had found the door to the house they had been staying in open, she said, despite the freezing conditions.

With drones buzzing overhead, Lina said she had not dared look inside, but had later heard from neighbours that my grandparents had been found dead. She believed it had been the Ukrainian soldiers who visited her house who had shot them.
Another neighbour, who I will call Maria, described discovering their bodies - my grandmother in bed, covered in a blanket, and my grandfather lying on the floor in a pool of now-dried blood.
Maria also believed Ukrainian soldiers had killed them - because, she said, that she too had felt threatened by Ukrainian troops at the time.
"If they had seen me they would have killed me too."
Her theory was that my grandparents had irritated the troops in some way.

"Your grandparents caught them in a bad mood because your grandfather was always asking to be evacuated. And [the soldiers] were, you know, high. They were taking drugs. So your grandparents got in their way," she told me.
Most of the other people in the village I spoke to also believe Ukrainian soldiers killed them, though their testimony is not based on direct evidence.

The new local mayor, appointed by the Russian occupiers when they finally took control of Dachne in February, said she had been present at my grandparents' burial the following month, and said half of my grandmother's skull was missing.
These accounts of how they might have died in January 2025 were deeply disturbing, though no-one had witnessed their deaths and the information I was given could not be independently verified.

The villagers I spoke to - now living in occupied territory - did say there had been some tensions between themselves and Ukrainian troops at the time, because the soldiers had viewed those who remained in Dachne as supporters of Russia.
The clinical causes of my grandparents' deaths are unclear.
Their bodies were not exhumed for nearly 20 months, when the local authorities sent them to a morgue in the occupied region, where a basic autopsy was carried out by a forensics expert.
He told me that my grandmother had died of an explosives injury to the skull - but could not specify its cause.
As for my grandfather, it said his body had shown no obvious signs of injury.

I compared two satellite images of the house in which their bodies were found - from just before and just after when they are believed to have died - and could detect no significant damage to the building in the second image.
I also spoke to a villager who said he had buried my grandparents.
He said he did not know anything about who killed them.
"I wasn't there. But why would you kill old people?" he asked.

I examined military maps from DeepStateMap.Live, an open-source Ukrainian resource, and US think tank Institute for the Study of War. They suggested Ukrainian forces still held the street where my grandparents lived during the week they had died, although the front line had been shifting rapidly.
My colleagues helped me identify the Russian military units that went on to capture Dachne. We found telephone numbers of Russian soldiers. But none of them agreed to speak to me.
I turned to the Ukrainian military.

A soldier from the 33rd Mechanised Brigade, who gave his name simply as Vlad, said his unit had still been in Dachne at the time my grandparents were believed to have died and that the Russians had been swiftly advancing.
Another Ukrainian soldier I spoke to also confirmed Ukraine's troops had still been in control of some parts of Dachne in late January.
We put our findings on the deaths of my grandparents to the Ukrainian military.

It said it had no verified evidence on how they died, or which implicated its servicemen during the "intense hostilities". It added that investigating allegations of wrongdoing was the role of law enforcement.
We also approached Russia's Ministry of Defence and Russia's embassy in London for comment - they did not respond.

The Donetsk regional prosecutor's office, which is now based outside Russian-controlled territory, has documented alleged Russian war crimes reported by eyewitnesses in villages around Dachne during December 2024 and January 2025 - including the killing of five civilians in a basement in the nearby village of Kostyantynopilske.
However, Ukrainian investigators have no equivalent cases registered in Dachne during that period. They have documented only three deaths there. My father and grandparents are not among them.
Their bodies lie in occupied territory, and I do not know if I will ever be able to say goodbye properly and bury them with dignity.
There is little more I can do for them, except one thing - mend my relationship with my sister and my mother.
Almost three years after I last saw my sister, I fly to Belgrade where she now lives.

She is waiting for me at the airport, holding lilies, and a plate with a silly nickname on it that she gave me when we were children. We hug, cry and laugh. It feels as if something between us is finally falling back into place
At her flat, we look through family photographs and talk about my investigation and what I was able to find. My grief is still there, but it hurts a little less. I'm no longer carrying it alone.
"Are you ready?" Sasha asks. She rings our mother - who has also moved to Serbia - and puts the phone on speaker.
"Hi, Mum. It's Nastya," I say. First there is silence. Then I hear her crying. "Nastya, my darling, hello," she replies.

articles.title: US preparing to unveil plan for new tariffs on global trading partners
articles.summary: The new levies would hit many of America's biggest trading partners, including China and the EU.

blocks.text: The US is preparing to announce plans for new tariffs on several countries as early as Wednesday, the BBC understands.
The new import taxes would hit many of America's biggest trading partners, with China, the European Union and Japan among at least 14 jurisdictions affected.

The move comes after the White House's so-called "Section 301" investigation. It was launched in March after the US Supreme Court ruled that President Donald Trump's Liberation Day tariffs were illegal.
Trump has made tariffs a signature policy of his presidency, arguing that they will help boost American manufacturing and create jobs.
The president sent shockwaves around the world when he unveiled sweeping tariffs on global trading partners in April 2025 shortly after his return to the White House.
While the tariffs were later struck down, US Trade Representative Jamieson Greer argued then that overproduction abroad was displacing American manufacturing and deterring investment.
Under the new tariffs, countries will face different import tax rates depending on the deals that they have previously struck with Trump.
The announcement is likely to increase tensions between the US and China, the world's two biggest economies, which remain locked in a trade dispute.
Despite last week's meeting between Trump and President Xi Jinping, the two sides have yet to fully resolve their difference with an interim agreement set to expire on 10 January.

articles.title: Kilmar Ábrego García, man at center of Trump deportation battle, leaving US
articles.summary:
Salvadorian man, who was deported in March 2025 and returned to US after supreme court ruling, leaving of own volition for Spain

Kilmar Ábrego García is leaving the United States of his own…
articles.byline: Cris Seda Chabrier in New York

blocks.text: Kilmar Ábrego García is leaving the United States of his own volition, his lawyers confirmed on Tuesday.
Ábrego is leaving the US for Spain on Tuesday evening.

The Salvadorian immigrant was at the center of a months-long legal battle since he was deported to El Salvador in March 2025 by the Trump administration, in defiance of a court’s protection. He was held in Cecot, a notorious anti-terrorism mega-prison.

He was ultimately returned to the US following a decision by the supreme court three months later. Since then, Ábrego has been fighting a second deportation to a series of African countries proposed by Department of Homeland Security (DHS) officials.
The Washington Post reported earlier on Tuesday that he negotiated a deal with federal authorities to depart the US voluntarily in order to avoid being forcibly removed.

In a statement, the US senator Chris Van Hollen, who has advocated for Maryland resident Ábrego and who met with him in El Salvador last year, described him as a “free man” and referenced Ábrego’s agreement with the Trump administration.

“While the Trump Administration had been pursuing their vindictive prosecution against Kilmar and desperately trying to ship him against his will to countries known for human rights abuses, the Administration was forced to come to this agreement that respects Kilmar’s will and the due process rights guaranteed to him and to all in our nation,” Van Hollen said. “I am relieved that he will be safe, in a country of his choosing, and free – including from this Administration’s constant persecution.”

The 31-year-old has an American wife and child and has lived in Maryland for years, but he immigrated to the US illegally as a teenager. In 2019, an immigration judge ruled that he could not be deported to El Salvador because he faced danger there from a gang that had threatened his family. The judge allowed him to live and work in the US under Immigration and Customs Enforcement supervision, but he was not given residency status.

He was arrested in Baltimore in March 2025 and deported to a Salvadorian prison in what an official later called an “administrative error”. Facing public pressure and a court order, the Trump administration brought him back in June 2025, but only after securing an indictment charging him with human smuggling in Tennessee. A federal judge dismissed that case in May, finding that the justice department’s pursuit of criminal charges was designed to punish Ábrego García for challenging his deportation. The government is appealing.
The Trump administration vowed to deport him to a third country, threatening to send him to Uganda, Eswatini, Ghana and, most recently, Liberia.

“We will always admire his remarkable courage in staring down and defeating a vindictive prosecution instigated by the highest reaches of the Justice Department,” one of Ábrego García’s attorneys, Sean Hecker, said in a statement provided to the Washington Post. “He, in turn, is grateful to those who stood by him.”
The Associated Press contributed

articles.title: Meerkats travel in packs. But they also make great solo navigators, researchers have found
articles.summary: When it comes to animals that travel in groups, like meerkats, it can be hard to tell how much they're navigating based on collective wisdom versus individual knowledge. So researchers separated…

image.caption: Researchers put GPS collars on meerkats at the Kalahari Research Centre in South Africa, separated them from their clans, and tracked them as they navigated their way home. (Mathilde Martin)

blocks.text: As It Happens·New

When it comes to animals that travel in groups, like meerkats, it can be hard to tell how much they're navigating based on collective wisdom versus individual knowledge. So researchers separated meerkats from their clans to see if they could find their way home.
Separated from their clans, most meerkats journeyed 1.5 kilometres to find their way home
Don't let Disney's The Lion King fool you. Meerkats don't hang out with warthogs, and they have plenty of worries — like finding enough delicious grubs to eat and fending off predators.
But the African critters handle whatever life throws at them by working together. They burrow together, raise their babies together and forage for food together.

Because of their co-operative nature, scientists figured they also relied on each other, to some degree, to navigate their terrain, with the more experienced travellers mapping the area and guiding the others.
But it turns out that most meerkats, when separated from their group, can find their way home all by themselves.

"They were very good at navigating," said University of Zurich biologist Mathilde Martin, lead author of a new study into meerkat solo navigation published in the Journal of Experimental Biology. "It was surprising."
Initial confusion

Meerkats are members of the mongoose family who live in groups of roughly 30 to 50 known as clans or mobs. They live in southern Africa, primarily in arid climates like deserts, savannas and grasslands.
Clanmates are rarely apart — that is, until Martin and her colleagues came along.

The researchers put GPS collars on 20 meerkats from five clans at the Kalahari Research Centre in South Africa. Then, one at a time, they gently scooped up the collared critters, put them in bags and released them 1.5 kilometres from their burrows.
Most of the meerkats made it back on their home without assistance. (Submitted by Mathilde Martin)
At first, Martin says, the relocated meerkats were confused.
"They needed a bit of time to calm down and think about what happened to them," she told As It Happens host Nil Kӧksal.
But once they got their wits about them, she says, they explored their new surroundings and charted a course home.
"When they started committing to a direction, they were very good at navigating," she said.
Eighteen of the meerkats made it home and reunited with their clans, she said, while two remained frozen in place.
"For ethical obvious reasons, we didn't want them to stay away from their group for too long," Martin said. "So after 90 minutes, we took them back to the group."
Males aren't necessarily better navigators, study finds
So why abduct innocent meerkats and separate them from their clans?
When it comes to animals who live collectively, the study says it can be hard to distinguish between group wisdom and individual knowledge.
The purpose of the study was to "disentangle what individuals know on their own from how such information is incorporated into collective movement decisions."
Researchers didn't find any difference between age and sex when it came to meerkats' ability to navigate solo. (Submitted by Mathilde Martin)
Martin says she expected adult males to make better navigators because of their tendency to go "roving."
"Some time during their life, [they] leave the group and seek for mating opportunities," she said. "And, so, they do solo navigation in their natural environment without those experiments."
Females, by contrast, "usually stay with their group their whole life," she said.
But, in the experiment, the females didn't spend any longer than the males exploring their drop-off point before heading in the right direction.
"We thought maybe they were a bit less good at navigating on their own, because they don't need to learn this and they could rely on their group," Martin said. "But they were great."
Pregnant females can get expelled from clan
Christine Drea, who has studied meerkat reproduction strategies, wasn't surprised. She says female meerkats aren't always so tight-knit.
Meerkat clans, she says, tend to have a dominant female who doesn't want her offspring to have any competition when it comes to collective babysitting.
"Usually, when a subordinate gets pregnant, she represents a threat," said Drea, a Duke University anthropologist who wasn't involved in the navigation study.
"And then the dominant female targets her for aggression until she's expelled from the group. She's basically sent off to the gulag."
Pregnant meerkats, she says, don't fare well on their own.
"She can't raise them by herself and feed herself, so her young are doomed to die," Drea said. "And once they die, once she's no longer pregnant, she also can go back to the clan."

items: These tiny endangered raccoons make their own toys out of trash
The 1st Fat Marmot Week winner is a 'special boy who likes to eat rocks'

blocks.text: Still, the study notes, when females are expelled they remain just outside the periphery of the clan, while males roam farther from home.
The study also found no difference in navigational skills based on age. Even younger meerkats who had no prior roaming or expulsion experience made it home.
How they did it, Martin says, remains to be discovered. But she's glad her research is spreading some knowledge of meerkats beyond what can be gleaned from Timon and Pumba.
"The picture we have of meerkat is this mongoose in The Lion King that is a solitary individual that doesn't live with a group and other individuals. And that's very wrong," Martin said.
Interview with Mathilde Martin produced by Livia Dyring

articles.title: After striking out on the top free agent (again), the Blue Jays turn to Japan
articles.summary: CBC Sports' daily newsletter breaks down the Toronto Blue Jays' signing of Japanese star Kaima Taira after they were turned down by the No. 1 player on the market.

image.caption: Newly acquired Blue Jays pitcher Kaima Taira played for Japan at the Tokyo Olympics and became a star in his country's version of the major leagues. (Kazuhiro Fujihara/AFP via Getty Images)

blocks.text: MLB·THE BUZZER
CBC Sports' daily newsletter breaks down the Toronto Blue Jays' signing of Japanese star Kaima Taira after they were turned down by the No. 1 player on the market.
Toronto moves on from Skubal by signing Seibu Lions star
The Buzzer Newsletter | This is a segment from CBC's weekday sports newsletter. | Sign up here to receive full versions of The Buzzer directly in your inbox.
For four straight years now, the Toronto Blue Jays have been "in on" the top player in free agency, only to come up short.

During the Shohei Ohtani mania of December 2023, online sleuths scoured everything from private jet flight paths to sushi restaurant reservations for clues before the modern-day Babe Ruth (predictably) turned down Toronto for a bigger offer from the Los Angeles Dodgers. In 2024, star outfielder Juan Soto chose the New York Mets, and last year Kyle Tucker joined Ohtani on the Dodgers.

The clear No. 1 free agent this off-season was Tarik Skubal, a 30-year-old left-handed starter who won back-to-back Cy Young Awards with Detroit before the non-contending Tigers sent him to the Dodgers at the trade-deadline in August. The Blue Jays were among a handful of teams making a serious effort to land Skubal and reportedly offered him a nine-year contract worth more than $400 million US. But the Mets, who had the biggest payroll in baseball this year, nabbed him on Sunday for nine years and $450M — the largest deal ever for a pitcher in terms of both total money and average annual value. (Interestingly, the famously free-spending Dodgers reportedly never made a formal offer amid owner Mark Walter's ongoing legal troubles.)
The good news is that, after getting outbid so many times, the Jays seem to have become pretty adept at refocusing on the other fish in the sea.

Last year, perhaps sensing that they weren't going to land Tucker and that shortstop Bo Bichette was not going to return on favourable terms (sure enough, he too signed with the Mets), Toronto proactively poached strikeout artist Dylan Cease from San Diego with a seven-year, $210M US contract. It turned out to be a savvy move as Cease led the American League in strikeout rate and finished second in Cy Young voting, though he did wear down as the season went on and ended up on the injured list with a shoulder issue that did not require surgery. Later, the Jays dipped into Japan to sign Kazuma Okamoto as their new third baseman, and he went on to lead the team with 33 home runs (more than double anyone else's total) despite striking out a ton.
Today, the Jays sort of blended those two signings, reportedly agreeing to a five-year, $80M contract with Japanese import Kaima Taira. It's their first big move of the off-season.

Taira is a 27-year-old right-handed starting pitcher who stands just 5-foot-8. As ESPN's excellent baseball writer Jeff Passan notes here, Taira is two inches shorter than any starter in Major League Baseball this year. But he weighs a solid 218 pounds and averaged a powerful 95.7 miles per hour on his fastball this season for the Seibu Lions, making him the hardest-throwing starter in Japan's version of the major leagues. He hit 100 mph on the radar gun this year, and he's said to deploy eight different types of pitches.

Taira, who played for Japan at the 2021 Olympics in Tokyo, spent six of his first pro seasons as a reliever before converting back to a starter this year. The Nippon Professional Baseball website shows he posted a miniscule 1.36 ERA in 146 innings while allowing just 95 hits, striking out 141 batters and walking 45. He also surrendered only four home runs.

If his effectiveness translates to the majors, Taira could give Toronto a formidable top three starters alongside Cease and Trey Yesavage, the 2025 playoff sensation who was derailed by injuries this year. And it's possible that the Jays are not done yet.
Other pitching options dwindling

Jays GM Ross Atkins may have felt pressure to sign Taira after some other possible Plan B starting pitchers went off the market over the last 24 hours. Former Baltimore left-hander Trevor Rogers reportedly agreed to an unexpectedly large five-year, $120M contract with the Chicago Cubs last night and, earlier today, the Orioles replaced Rogers by luring righty Freddy Peralta from Tampa Bay with a reported five-year, $125M deal.

If the Jays want to make further upgrades to their rotation, they could look to the likes of Michael King, a crafty 32-year-old right-hander who had a 132 ERA+ (meaning he was 32 per cent better than the league average) for San Diego this year; Tyler Mahle, another 32-year-old righty who posted a 1.99 ERA after being traded to Atlanta at the August deadline; or even 35-year-old Kevin Gausman, who was Toronto's ace for a few years before they shipped him to the Cubs that same day as they slipped out of contention. If the Jays are looking to shore up their bullpen, the top guy on the market is flamethrowing lefty Adrian Morejon, who struck out 11.2 batters per nine innings this year with the Padres and is viewed by some as a potential starter.
What about the bats?

But we all know that pitching was not the reason the Jays went from being one play away from winning the World Series against the mighty Dodgers to finishing dead last in the AL East. Toronto ranked ninth in the majors in team ERA this year — up from 19th in 2025.

The main causes of Toronto's downfall, besides a slew of injuries to key players, came at the plate. While the Jays still hit for a pretty good average and were very difficult to strike out, they plummeted from No. 1 in the majors in on-base percentage in 2025 down to a three-way tie for 25th while experiencing a stunning power outage. Among the 30 big-league teams, Toronto finished last in home runs (they were 11th in 2025) and 26th in slugging percentage (down from seventh). As a result, they scored a major-league-low 648 runs — more than 200 fewer than the MLB-leading Cubs.

The poster boy for Toronto's anemic offence was Vladimir Guerrero Jr., who went from the toast of Canada with his eight homers in 18 post-season games in 2025 to mustering just nine in 144 games this year, including a grand total of one at home. Vladdy also posted the lowest batting average and slugging percentage of his eight-year career and his worst on-base percentage for a full season.

Seeing as how Guerrero was worth a pretty inconsequential 1.1 Wins Above Replacement this year, a generous person could argue that a return to form by the superstar slugger would basically amount to a big free-agent acquisition. A less-generous person might say that Guerrero better bounce back because he still has 13 years left on the titanic 14-year, $500M extension he signed in April 2025.

But that's all spilled milk under the bridge. If the Jays don't want to just bank on a quick rebound by Guerrero and the rest of the everyday lineup, they have some options to add a bat in free agency.

One potential spot to target is the corner outfield, where the options include Seiya Suzuki, who averaged 29 homers the last two years with the Cubs; and Randy Arozarena, a rookie sensation with Tampa a few years ago who had 26 homers and 26 stolen bases this season for Seattle. But a big piece came off the board today when Japanese league MVP Teruaki Sato agreed to a reported six-year, $120M deal with the Cubs as Chicago continued its spending spree.

There's also the middle infield. If the Jays aren't sold on Ernie Clement at second base (we all love him, but his .285 on-base percentage this year left a lot to be desired), they might consider the Yankees' Jazz Chisholm Jr. He racked up 31 homers and 31 steals in 2025 and, despite regressing at the plate this year, remained a valuable player with his high-quality baserunning and defence. Another candidate at second is Pittsburgh's Brandon Lowe, who improved his weak defensive play this year while reaching the 30-homer plateau for the second straight time. But he also strikes out a lot, which the Jays don't like.
Lockout looming

Whatever direction the Jays choose, they may have to act fast. The current collective bargaining agreement expires one week from tonight, at which point the owners will almost certainly lock out the players and all business will be suspended until a new CBA is hammered out.
That could take awhile. The owners are hell-bent on getting a salary cap for the first time in baseball history, while the players are very much against it.

At the moment, there's little urgency to make a deal as spring training is still 2½ months away and Opening Day is four months from today. Both sides know those are the real deadlines, so we're still in the sabre-rattling and exchanging-half-hearted-proposals stage.

But, judging by all the big signings that have gone down in the last few days, teams are clearly feeling the heat to make moves before the big shutdown. We'll see whether the Blue Jays stay in on the action.
